## I Blew Up A Secret Business To Prove It's Not Luck
`SmiOK8Yun4s` · https://youtu.be/SmiOK8Yun4s

*Teardown of a fashion stylist doing $309K a year: fix the leaky funnel (lead magnet, VSSL, harder qualification, headline), scale the affiliate channel she was ignoring (6 partners already produced a third of revenue), and reprice with a high-end anchor and a default back-end.*

### Case study

**Business.** Ashley's fashion styling business - personal styling and design advice for high-income clients (CEOs, socialites, frequent flyers) with a $8,500 60-day onboarding, continuity, and 10% affiliate commission on clothing

**Starting state.** $309,000 revenue and $130,000 profit last year (42% margins), over 1,000 lifetime customers. Paid cold traffic went to a form with no headline, no value proposition and a 'get more info' button: 1,800 clicks produced 8 sales. No lead magnet, no video sales letter, no qualification. Six affiliates (found by a basic Google search and 40 emails) produced a third of the business. Most clients were grandfathered at $1,500/quarter or less, only a couple paid the $2,000/month tier, and no pricing was…

**Diagnosis.** Three constraints. (1) A leaky funnel - the bottleneck is conversion, not traffic, and it leaks because there is no reason to opt in and no qualification. (2) A missed gold mine - a channel already proven to work (6 affiliates, one-third of revenue, $2,500 of revenue per email sent) was being run at almost zero volume. (3) Pricing - no price anchor, no frictionless upsell from onboarding into continuity, and a premium brand delivered through a commodity sales process, so the frame breaks and conversion drops. He also places her at stage four of the scaling roadmap: identify and double down on…

**Intervention.**

- Funnel, step 1: add a lead magnet - a personalized style assessment (skin tone, body type, lifestyle) qualified on BANT plus income, since it is high-touch concierge work, not an ebook
- Funnel, step 2: install a VSSL - a 3-7 minute video that pre-frames the assessment and pre-sells the call; built by recording answers to the most common objections from sales recordings and sending it to every prospect in the funnel
- Funnel, step 3: qualify harder - BANT plus an income question in the intake form so unqualified buyers are filtered before she creates a personalized assessment
- Funnel, step 4: rewrite the headline and subheadline around the freebie: 'free lookbook to dress for your tone using your existing closet' (the 'using your existing closet' kills the biggest objection)
- Affiliates, step 1: build the list beyond matchmakers - private social clubs, executive coaches, high-end personal trainers, divorce attorneys - anyone whose customers are in the buying moment (recently divorced, newly single executives, wives whose husbands' dress does not match their status)
- Affiliates, step 2: send the emails - 400 in 30 days, 20 per day, no fancy software
- Affiliates, step 3: activate and retain - treat affiliates like customers, farm the relationship (dinners, events hosted for their customers, sponsorship that makes the affiliate look good)
- Pricing, step 1: introduce a highest-tier continuity option (about 10x) so the $2,000/month and $4,500/quarter look reasonable, keeping the anchor similar to the core offer with only one or two differences nobody cares about
- Pricing, step 2: make the back-end the default next step after onboarding ('you have already invested in your transformation, let's make sure it sticks')
- Pricing, step 3: keep pushing price until the conversion drop costs more than the price gain - the point of maximum profit is after the point of maximum conversion

**Result.** No measured results are given in this video - the fixes are presented as a plan. His estimates: the funnel rebuild (lead magnet, VSSL, qualification, headline) could give her 2-3x, and if only 10% of clients take a high-end anchor priced at 10x, it effectively doubles the revenue of the business.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting revenue and profit | **$309,000 revenue, $130,000 profit, 42% margins** |
| Funnel leak | **1,800 clicks to 8 sales** |
| Affiliate concentration | **six partners send a third of her entire business** |
| Affiliate expansion goal | **40 emails to date to 400 emails in 30 days (20/day), 6…** |
| Price anchor effect | **10% take at 10x price doubles revenue** |
| Estimated funnel fix effect | **2-3x** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Three moves, in this order. (1) Before buying more traffic, stop the leak: give a narrow, qualified free thing, add a short pre-call video built from recorded objections, and qualify with BANT so unqualified people never consume your delivery time. (2) Hunt the gold mine already inside the business - find the channel that produced outsized results and do 10x more of it (here: 40 emails had produced 6 partners worth a third of revenue, so the instruction was 400 emails in 30 days, plus a relationship owner to keep partners activated). (3) Then reprice: add a high anchor about 10x the core…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The affiliate numbers are the actionable part and are usually left out: 6 partners found by 40 emails produced one-third of revenue, worth $2,500 per email sent, so the prescribed move was 400 emails in 30 days at 20/day with a named list of adjacent business types (private social clubs, executive…
- The pricing mechanics are stated as a calculation: a 10x anchor taken by only 10% of clients doubles revenue, and the anchor should stay similar to the core offer with one or two differences nobody cares about.
- Unlike the other teardowns in this batch, this video gives no measured after-numbers - the results are projections (2-3x from the funnel fixes), so it should not be cited as a proven outcome.
- The transcript states '4% conversion to traffic' while the same passage gives 8 sales from 1,800 clicks (under 1%) - the two figures cannot both be right.

## If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview
`YZdE8U5eD_s` · https://youtu.be/YZdE8U5eD_s

*Harley Finkelstein (Shopify) explains how a snowboard shop's software became a ~$100B company: grow the pie rather than take a slice, be more generous than the incumbents (80/20 app store rev share, 20% in perpetuity to referral partners), and build for 100 years.*

### Case study

**Business.** Shopify - the e-commerce platform Tobi Lütke started in 2005 and Harley Finkelstein joined, told here by Harley (third-party case study in an interview, not a Hormozi teardown)

**Starting state.** In 2005 there were two ways to sell online: a marketplace, where you rent your customers, or enterprise software costing a couple of million dollars. Tobi Lütke, a programmer who had moved from Germany to Canada, wanted to build a snowboard shop on the internet and wrote his own software in Ruby on Rails rather than accept either option. Harley became one of the first merchants in 2006 (when the product was called Jaded Pixel) and joined the company around 2009 while also acting as its lawyer.

**Diagnosis.** The strategic constraint was not product but ecosystem and trust: a platform only wins if the people building on it make money, so the decisions that mattered were about being more generous than incumbents and letting partners carry distribution. Harley names three decisions from the first ten years: the app store and ecosystem (which gave 100% product-market fit across use cases and a distributed salesforce not on payroll), the Build-a-Business competition (which created new merchants and press), and Merchant Solutions (negotiating payment rates in aggregate as if they were the…

**Intervention.**

- Write the software rather than rent customers from a marketplace or pay millions for enterprise software
- Build an app store and set the developer revenue share at 80/20 when the incumbent (Apple's iOS store) was 70/30 - more generous than the incumbents
- Run the Build-a-Business competition with Tim Ferriss (launched 2010) with a $100,000 prize they did not yet have, generating new merchants and a New York Times article
- Pay referral partners 20% of what Shopify took, in perpetuity, turning agencies into a recurring cash-flow channel
- Use aggregate merchant size to negotiate payment gateway rates as if they were the second-largest retailer, then pass most of the benefit to merchants
- Hold to a merchant-obsessed mission as the single heuristic so thousands of employees can decide independently
- Think in decades - explicitly building a 100-year business, which meant patience over short-term extraction
- Divest businesses that are not 'main quests' (e.g. Shopify Fulfillment Network)
- Grow the pie rather than take a slice of it

**Result.** IPO in May 2015 on the NYSE at about a $1 billion valuation - roughly 1% of today's market cap. In 2022 Shopify did $5.6 billion of revenue while its merchants generated almost $200 billion of GMV, and ecosystem partners earned more than $6 billion. By the time of this interview Shopify was worth around $100 billion with 8,000-9,000 employees. Harley's recurring finding from interviewing entrepreneurs in their 80s and 90s (about 12 interviews, including Izzy Sharp of Four Seasons at 95) is that…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Value of Shopify | **about $100 billion** |
| IPO | **May 2015, a $1B company then** |
| 2022 revenue vs merchant volume | **$5.6B revenue vs ~$200B GMV, partners made more than $6B** |
| App store rev share choice | **80/20 vs the incumbent's 70/30** |
| Referral partner share | **20% in perpetuity** |
| Headcount | **eight or nine thousand people at the company** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Build the ecosystem, not just the product: give partners a reason to sell for you (80/20 rev share when the incumbent offered 70/30; 20% in perpetuity to referrers), run a competition that manufactures new customers and press before you can afford the prize, and use aggregate scale to negotiate rates your individual customers could never get. Two operating rules underneath it: one simple heuristic everyone can apply independently (merchant obsessed), and a decade-long time horizon (a 100-year business) that lets you refuse anything that is not a main quest. The check on whether you are doing…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The partner economics are stated numerically and are the actionable part: 80/20 app store revenue share against the incumbent's 70/30, 20% in perpetuity to referral partners, and a $100,000 competition prize announced before they could afford it.
- The scale evidence is given: 2022 revenue $5.6B against ~$200B of merchant GMV and more than $6B earned by ecosystem partners, with an IPO in May 2015 at about $1B (roughly 1% of the value at interview time).
- This is an interview, not a teardown - the case study is Shopify's history as told by Harley Finkelstein, and there is no before/after intervention on a third-party business. Two figures are corrupted in the auto-captions ('100100 million' Series B valuation and Shopify's share of the 46 million…

## I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)
`c_6BrF7jOGk` · https://youtu.be/c_6BrF7jOGk

*A portfolio company run by three young founders is fixed by five changes in a strict order - hire a sales director first, then fix ad targeting, then cut the sales team and raise setter expectations, then split lead nurture into its own role, then rescript discovery - and the funnel math goes from 56 to 93 sales a month in 60 days.*

### Case study

**Business.** One of Hormozi's 13 portfolio companies - a two-call-close, mid-priced consumer service run by three young founders, with a separate setting team and closing team (Part 1 covers the sales and marketing side; product and customer success are deferred to Part 2)

**Starting state.** Prior month: 56 units sold. 49% show rate, 83% offer rate, 27% close rate, 47% of cash collected up front. Ads were optimized for lowest cost per lead/appointment and targeting 18-24 year olds instead of the intended 25-35 year olds who love their job, forcing 75% of appointments to be cancelled before the 49% show rate. Setters both cold-called and nurtured, with no double dialing, speed-to-contact of 30 minutes to 3 hours, and no day-of reminder. The CEO was the sales manager because he was…

**Diagnosis.** Five problems, in the order he ranks them: (1) low show rate from wrong ad targeting and no nurture; (2) multitasking - the same setters were prospecting and nurturing; (3) low close rate from surface-level discovery ('how much money do you want to make' instead of intention-based why questions) which produced objections in the close; (4) people and org structure - the CEO was the sales manager, and the setter benchmark was set too low at 2 a day; (5) and the root 'who' problem: a negligent media buyer optimizing for the wrong thing. He is explicit that the sequencing matters: the sales…

**Intervention.**

- Hire an experienced sales director (a former sales trainer for a similar consumer sale) to take over from the CEO - done first, because everything else would have fallen flat without it
- Fix ad targeting: let go of the media buyer who was asleep at the wheel, and switch optimization from cost per lead/appointment to cost per sale, restoring the 25-35 audience
- Reduce the sales team size and raise setter expectations: cut the lowest closing percentage, reset the daily set expectation from 2 to 4
- Promote one setter to lead nurture specialist to act as the bridge between the setting and closing teams, with a checklist (three-way intro between setter and closer, day-of personalized voice memo or video text from the closer)
- Rescript discovery: deeper why/intention questions instead of surface-level ones, pre-empt objections before the close (including asking before the appointment whether anyone else must be involved in the decision, and pushing the appointment back if so), and drill the team on looping

**Result.** In 60 days: show rate 49% to 70% (a 40% improvement, essentially hitting the 70% KPI); offer rate roughly unchanged at about 80% because they had been offering unqualified people; close rate 27% to 41% (a 50% improvement, 1% above the benchmark); cash collected up front 47% to 82%, nearly doubling cash per sale; and units sold went from 56 to 93 per month - which compounds to roughly 4x cash flow.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting state | **56 units sold in the prior month** |
| Show rate after the fixes | **70%** |
| Close rate after the fixes | **41%** |
| Cash collected up front after the fixes | **82%** |
| Units per month after the fixes | **93** |
| Net cash flow effect | **4x** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Measure the funnel as a chain (show rate, offer rate, close rate, cash collected up front, units) so the constraint is arithmetic rather than opinion, then fix in order of dependency: the person first, then the traffic quality, then the team's expectations and size, then the script. Two rules to copy: if the same problem recurs in the same department under the same person, it is a who problem not a what problem; and when salespeople have too few calls they get desperate and push, while with enough calls they sell from the back of their heel - so cutting the lowest performers and raising…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The video gives the funnel as an auditable chain with benchmarks per step (70% show, ~40% close for a two-call mid-priced consumer service, cash-collected-up-front as a conviction metric) - generic summaries say 'improve your funnel' without the per-step targets or the arithmetic.
- The sequencing claim is specific and falsifiable: the sales director hire came first because without it the other four changes would have failed, and he frames hiring errors as one of the biggest costs in a business (time to find, onboard, train, discover the misfit, and restart).
- Result numbers are stated as before/after pairs: 49% to 70% show, 27% to 41% close, 47% to 82% cash up front, 56 to 93 units a month, roughly 4x cash flow - all inside 60 days.

## Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]
`gN--zZi3Nfc` · https://youtu.be/gN--zZi3Nfc

*Once you know the tactics, the constraint stops being information and becomes hunger - so when a business stalls, the job is to find and attack the reason you are not doing the thing you already know you should do.*

### Case study

**Business.** Gym owners (Gym Launch clients / his mastermind members) - several established operators with low sales show rates

**Starting state.** Gym owners near or at seven figures, in business for years, complaining that their show rates were low. They claimed to be doing the reminders and follow-up.

**Diagnosis.** Not a tactics problem. Digging one level deeper, the gym was only open one hour per day (7:15 a.m.) for new-client appointments, so prospective customers could never book. He frames this as the symptom of a bigger problem: they had made it in their own mind, got comfortable and lost their hunger, so the obvious hole went unaddressed. A second gym was available only 9-11 a.m. on weekdays - the hours when the people with money are working.

**Intervention.**

- Audit the obvious hole first - availability, not reminders or scripts
- Open appointment availability to the hours clients can actually attend, not the hours convenient to the owner
- Once the tactical hole is found, spend the session on why the owner is not doing it, not on more tactics
- Use the fear test: if your family's life depended on getting more clients, would you be available one hour a day?

**Result.** No measured result is given for these owners - the point is diagnostic. He states that once the tactics are known (e.g. after joining Gym Launch, where you learn how to make a seven-figure gym), the failure reflects back on the owner, and 'the tactics aren't the thing anymore'.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Availability window set by the complaining gym for new clients | **one hour per day at 7:15 a.m.** |
| Availability window of a second gym | **9:00 a.m. to 11 a.m.** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When a business stalls and the fix is already known, stop shopping for tactics and audit execution capacity first: can a customer actually buy at a time they are available? Then treat the owner's refusal to do the known thing as the real constraint, and attack that reason rather than the tactic. The test he uses to expose it: if your family's survival depended on this, would you still be available one hour a day?

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Summaries of this talk usually keep the motivation message and drop the concrete audit he describes: the diagnostic was availability (one hour per day at 7:15 a.m.; another gym 9-11 a.m.), which is checkable rather than inspirational.
- He gives a specific order of operations for coaching calls - find the obvious tactical hole, then spend the next hour and a half on why the owner is not doing it - which is absent from the written framework summaries.

## How to Get Rich [Full Interview with Dave Ramsey]
`jvXOOddDg_s` · https://youtu.be/jvXOOddDg_s

*Dave Ramsey walks through the construction of a $300M business from a free radio show and a self-published book - one profit center at a time, a trade of MBA strategy for work ethic, and a rule that organizations never outgrow the character and intellectual capacity of their leadership.*

### Case study

**Business.** Ramsey Solutions - Dave Ramsey's company (third-party case study told by Ramsey in an interview with Hormozi)

**Starting state.** Ramsey started broke after a personal bankruptcy at 26 with $1.2M of called notes. He worked for free at a Chapter 11 talk radio station in Nashville, self-published his first book in 1992 (1,000 copies carried home in the trunk of his car), and moved out of his living room into an 800 sq ft month-to-month office 18 months later. His first class in April 1994 drew 4 people, of whom he sold 3.

**Diagnosis.** Two constraints, both non-financial. (1) The product insight: personal finance is 80% behavior and 20% head knowledge, so the product had to be education plus accountability, not information. (2) The leadership constraint: 'organizations are not going to outgrow the character and intellectual capacity of their leadership' - so his own limits set the ceiling, which is why he traded with the MBAs on his team (they taught him strategic thought, he taught them how to work) about 20 years ago.

**Intervention.**

- Use free radio as the megaphone, not the product - it produced no revenue but fed everything else
- Build one profit center at a time (book/publishing, live events, the class that became Financial Peace University, then high-school curriculum, workplace curriculum, EntreLeadership, EveryDollar, Ramsey Trusted endorsements) - about 14 profit centers over roughly 35 years
- Reposition the class as Financial Peace University five to six months after the first version and push it through churches
- Trade with his own team: MBAs teach strategic thought, he teaches work
- Buy real estate and hold it in entity structures (the campus sits in a Children's Trust with the company as tenant)
- Refuse debt and refuse to risk the empire for a pot of gold; risk-adjust every investment by the volatility taken on
- Pour resources into whatever channel shows results (e.g. Shorts) rather than following a fixed plan
- Never sell, never IPO - run the infinite game

**Result.** Ramsey Solutions now does a little over $300 million a year with about 1,100 employees, split roughly 40% Ramsey Trusted endorsements, 15% EntreLeadership, 15% Financial Peace University, under 10% EveryDollar. Financial Peace University has been taken by 10 million people and taught in 50,000 churches; the high-school curriculum is in 48% of US high schools; Smart Dollar has been taught at 10,000 companies including U-Haul and Costco.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue today | **a little over $300 million a year** |
| Where it started | **four people came the first night, he sold three of them** |
| Reach of the flagship product | **10 million people, 50,000 churches** |
| Revenue mix | **40% Ramsey Trusted, 15% EntreLeadership, 15% FPU, under 10%…** |
| The growth constraint he names | **the character and intellectual capacity of the leadership** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Build profit centers one at a time on top of a free attention mechanism: Ramsey used radio (zero revenue, pure megaphone) to feed publishing, live events and a class that became a 10-million-person product. Each new center gets tested cheaply, and the resources go where the response is. Two rules that make it work: fix your own limits first, because the business cannot outgrow the character and intellectual capacity of its leadership; and treat debt as identical to risk - risk-adjust the return before comparing it to anything else.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The revenue mix is given numerically here and is usually missing from summaries: ~$300M total, Ramsey Trusted ~40%, EntreLeadership ~15%, Financial Peace University ~15%, EveryDollar under 10%, with 1,100 employees and 8,000-9,000 endorsed professionals.
- The origin numbers make the scale legible: 1,000 self-published copies in 1992, a first class in April 1994 with 4 attendees of whom 3 bought, an 800 sq ft office, and a first live event of about 100 people at about $40 a ticket.
- The risk-adjustment argument is stated with actual betas and returns (0.8 growth-and-income fund vs 2.0 aggressive growth vs S&P 1.0; 20% return meeting an 11.2% return after risk adjustment) - the framework summaries state 'avoid debt' without the math.
- This is an interview, not a teardown: the case study is Ramsey's own company history, told by Ramsey, and no results are reported for any third-party business.

## Building a $1,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 56 Mins
`nrounb8NlFQ` · https://youtu.be/nrounb8NlFQ

*Full teardown of Ashley Kaps' luxury styling business AC Styles: the economics are already excellent (16:1 LTV:CAC, near-zero churn) so the only constraint is volume - fix the leaking paid funnel, then 10x the affiliate channel that already produces a third of revenue.*

### Case study

**Business.** AC Styles - Ashley Kaps' professional wardrobe and personal styling service for luxury clientele (moms/socialites with social calendars, and male CEOs; 50/50 men and women, 40s to mid-60s), with a 60-day $8,500 onboarding and monthly/quarterly continuity

**Starting state.** $309,000 revenue, $130,000 profit, 42% net margin, 4 years in business, 1,000+ clients served lifetime. 40 active clients with 1 churn in the last year. Current flow: 12 leads/month, 8 appointments, 100% show rate, 4 sales (50% close). Acquisition: Google AdWords at $300/month ($3,400 for 2024, $189 CPC, 1,800 clicks, 8 sales), Thumbtack at $300/month ($6,000 spend, 58 leads at $38, 8 sales, 90-95% unqualified), 6 affiliates (4 matchmakers + 2 private clubs) driving about a third of revenue,…

**Diagnosis.** The business is fundamentally healthy - 42% margins, 16:1 LTV:CAC, ~2.5% annual churn, 100% show rate, 50% close rate - so the constraint is volume ('the N is low'). Two things block volume: (1) the paid funnel leaks, because traffic lands on a page with no prices, no video and no reason to opt in - 1,800 clicks produced 8 sales, meaning she is only skimming people in dire pain; (2) the highest-leverage channel is running at a tenth of its proven rate - 6 affiliates found with 40 manual emails produce a third of revenue. Continuity and pricing are working, so he deliberately leaves them alone.

**Intervention.**

- Priority 1 - fix conversion before spending more: add a video sales letter plus a lead magnet (color/skin-tone analysis or 'one perfect outfit' - immediate, no work for the prospect), plus BANT qualification on the scheduler, plus skin tone/hair/eye personalization, plus attribution tracking
- Priority 2 - increase ad spend from $300/month to $600-900/month (he floats $3,400/month, which would be 12x) once the funnel and attribution are in place
- Priority 3 - the affiliate play: 20 emails a day (or 40 a day for a month) to 4 affiliate types (high-end trainers/PTs, executive coaches, dating people/matchmakers, divorce attorneys), plus one event per quarter to keep them activated
- Priority 4 - do not touch continuity: keep both the $2,000/month and $4,500/quarter tiers because the monthly tier works as a price anchor
- Sequencing rationale: the first two changes cost almost nothing (a PDF, a headline, a button click - half a day to a day) so they go first; the affiliate work requires weeks of manual outreach so it goes second
- Do not add Facebook ads - she already has a working acquisition channel, so spend more on what works instead
- Do not revisit the avatar split (moms vs male CEOs) yet - she genuinely likes both; revisit at $3M-$5M with more data

**Result.** No measured results in this video. His projections: fixing the funnel could be a 2-5x lift in lead flow (or 5-10x the sales); 10x-ing the affiliates takes a third of the business to a triple; combining a 2x and a 2x and a 3x gives a 12x, which would take the business from $300,000 a year to $3.6 million. He also sets the intermediate goal of tripling to $1M this year on the way to a $5M target.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting state | **309 [thousand] total revenue, 130 [thousand] profit, 42%…** |
| Paid funnel leak | **1,800 clicks, 8 sales** |
| Affiliate channel | **6 affiliates from 40 emails = one third of revenue…** |
| Projected affiliate effect | **10x of one third = more than tripling** |
| Combined projection | **12x, $300K to $3.6M** |
| Ad spend increase | **$300/month to $600-900/month** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Audit in this order: unit economics first (if LTV:CAC is 16:1 and churn is near zero, stop redesigning the business - the constraint is volume), then find the leaking step (1,800 clicks into 8 sales means the landing page has no reason to opt in), then find the point of leverage already proven inside the business (6 affiliates from 40 emails = a third of revenue) and 10x it rather than optimizing it, then fix the rest in the order of least effort first - the funnel fix is a PDF and a headline, the affiliate play is weeks of outreach, and the price/continuity work is left alone because it…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The video gives the actual acquisition economics per channel, which is what makes the diagnosis possible: Google $3,400/year at $189 CPC for 1,800 clicks and 8 sales; Thumbtack $6,000 for 58 leads at $38 with 90-95% unqualified; affiliates 40 emails to 6 partners for a third of revenue, $2,500 per…
- The ordering rule is explicit and usually lost in summaries: do the zero-cost, one-day changes first (lead magnet, headline, ad-spend button), then the multi-week manual work (affiliate outreach), and leave what already works (continuity and pricing) untouched.
- The continuity decision is counter-intuitive and quotable: keep the $2,000/month tier even though almost nobody takes it, because it anchors the $4,500/quarter and raises its take rate.
- This is a projection teardown - the $300K to $3.6M number is his model (2x funnel x 2x x 3x affiliate), not a measured outcome, and should not be cited as a result.

## We Broke The Guinness World Record In 24 Hours
`u3H7CfpfwHQ` · https://youtu.be/u3H7CfpfwHQ

*Behind the scenes of the $100 Million Money Models launch: a 24-hour live event built to break the fastest-selling non-fiction book record, run like an operation with a pre-mortem of every choke point and a phone team standing by at checkout.*

### Case study

**Business.** Acquisition.com's launch of the $100 Million Money Models book - a live 24-hour event with Guinness World Record judges present, selling the book for a $200 donation

**Starting state.** The record for the fastest-selling non-fiction book in a single day was held by Prince Harry at 1.4 million copies (before him, Barack Obama and Michelle Obama at around 750,000). These are globally recognized names with giant media machines behind them; Hormozi's team had no such media apparatus and one shot at a live 24-hour window.

**Diagnosis.** Two constraints. First, belief: nobody believes a claim like 'this can double your business' without proof, so the event itself had to be the proof - 'the best way to get someone to believe is to have already done it'. Second, execution: a live one-shot launch has a small number of choke points that can kill it, so they were enumerated in advance (ad platform throttling, email/SMS delivery, broken links, Shopify payment processing) with fallbacks for each.

**Intervention.**

- Package the $100M series as three books (offers, leads, money models) and launch them together so each stacks on the last
- Make the event itself the proof: a live 24-hour launch with Guinness judges on stage verifying the number
- Give the book away for a $200 donation with $31M of consulting work included
- Hire and train 300+ phone reps to help any buyer with checkout, and run role-play training on every offer
- Pre-mortem the failure modes: list every choke point in order and prevent each (link checks, Shopify test, email/SMS send verification)
- Have a fallback chain for paid traffic: when Google Ads went down, reroute budget to Meta, then TikTok, then LinkedIn
- Control the physical environment for the one-shot performance (curtains, dedicated camera, chat placed behind the presenter) and rehearse the flow repeatedly
- Keep calling until they could not call any more, then move to Australia as it woke up

**Result.** The record was broken inside the 24-hour window - the Guinness judges confirmed they were the new official record holder, with the previous record at 1.43 million copies and the final number to be confirmed the next morning. Live milestones along the way: cracked 200,000, running at 1,000 books a second, $2M before lunch, past $3M, plus a single buyer taking 10,000 books for his community.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Record being beaten | **1.4 million copies (Prince Harry)** |
| Record confirmed as broken | **1.43 million copies sold** |
| Value of consulting work included | **$31 million, book free with a $200 donation** |
| Phone reps hired and trained | **300 plus** |
| Peak velocity | **1,000 books a second** |
| Revenue milestones during the stream | **$2 million before lunch** |
| Single largest order in progress | **10,000 books** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Make the claim and the proof the same object: if the offer is extraordinary, run the event that demonstrates it live rather than asserting it. Operationally, treat a one-shot launch as a pre-mortem exercise - enumerate the choke points in order (ad platforms, email/SMS sends, links, checkout), have a fallback chain for each (Google Ads to Meta to TikTok to LinkedIn), staff the checkout with humans, and rehearse the physical performance until it is automatic. The result here: an unknown-brand author beat Prince Harry's 1.4M-copy single-day record by having the launch itself be the evidence.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The record numbers are stated precisely in the video - Prince Harry at 1.4M copies, the prior holder around 750,000, and the confirmed record at 1.43M copies - and the launch milestones (200,000 cracked, 1,000 books/second, $2M before lunch, $3M+) are only in the stream footage.
- The operational detail is the transferable part and is missing from summaries: a numbered choke-point list with fallback chains, 300+ trained phone reps, and the $200-donation pricing with $31M of consulting content given away.

## Interviewing a Billionaire + Revealing My Workout Routine [Ep 005]
`y7O-iTWwTW8` · https://youtu.be/y7O-iTWwTW8

*A behind-the-scenes episode where Hormozi flies to Nashville to interview Dave Ramsey, and the load-bearing lesson is Ramsey's portfolio advice: allocate to your own knowledge base (80% real estate / 20% stocks for Graham Stephan; all-business for Hormozi), which became the thesis behind Acquisition.com.*

### Case study 1

**Business.** Hormozi's investment portfolio / Acquisition.com - the decision of where to deploy business profits

**Starting state.** He had money to deploy and asked every rich person he knew what to do with it; the answers were as different as the people, which left him more confused than before.

**Diagnosis.** He was collecting other people's strategies instead of allocating to his own knowledge base. Dave Ramsey's advice to Graham Stephan ('your giftings are much more in the real estate world than they are in analyzing stocks... 80 real estate 20 stocks') reframed the question as: what is YOUR knowledge base?

**Intervention.**

- Ask what your own knowledge base is rather than copying what worked for others
- For Hormozi the answer was all business: stop diversifying into things he did not understand
- Stick to business and buy businesses and grow them

**Result.** That decision is what they did with Acquisition.com - putting money into stuff he understands and loves instead of stuff that sounds fancy.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Ramsey's suggested split for Graham Stephan's knowledge base | **80% real estate / 20% stocks** |
| Dave Ramsey's daily work volume over 30+ years | **three hours a day for 30 plus years** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Allocate capital (and your time) according to your own knowledge base, not according to what rich people say worked for them. Concretely: take the portfolio of what you actually understand and are good at, weight toward that, and buy/grow assets in that domain - Hormozi's version of '80/20' was 100% business, which became Acquisition.com.

### Case study 2

**Business.** Hormozi's content channel - a clip made for one stranger (captioned 'Avante' / Devonte) who stopped him while walking

**Starting state.** A young man working two jobs with a one-year-old, shaking, told him he was sick and tired of being poor and did not know how to get out. No audience research, just one person's problem.

**Diagnosis.** There are far more people struggling than succeeding, so content that speaks tactically to what to do when you are struggling reaches a much broader audience than content for people who are already winning.

**Intervention.**

- Record the answer to that one person's situation directly
- Keep it tactical rather than motivational - what to do when you are broke, not inspiration

**Result.** The clip went viral everywhere ('went crazy everywhere'); Hormozi says he was not surprised it got the response it did, and that it served far more people than the one stranger it was made for.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Age of the child of the stranger who approached him | **one-year-old** |
| Number of jobs the stranger was working | **two jobs** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Pick the largest struggling segment, not the segment you find most impressive, and answer one specific person's problem in tactical terms. The size of the audience is a function of how many people share the problem you are answering - Hormozi points out there are far more people struggling than succeeding, which is why a clip made for one broke stranger outperformed content aimed at established operators.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- This episode is usually filed as a vlog, but it contains the origin of the Acquisition.com thesis: Ramsey's 'invest in your knowledge base' advice (80/20 real estate/stocks for Graham Stephan) is what Hormozi applied to himself, concluding his knowledge base was business, not stocks or real estate.
- The Devonte clip (captioned 'Avante' in the auto-captions) is the content case study - a video made for one struggling stranger that went viral - and it is the reason the channel's tactical content targets people who are struggling rather than people already winning.
- The auto-captions render the stranger's name as 'Avante'; Hormozi refers to him as Devonte. Quote text preserves the caption spelling.

## How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke
`by3ZEoo-Quc` · https://youtu.be/by3ZEoo-Quc

*Four sources of money - past (savings), income, debt (future earnings) and 'new money' - and the behaviour of funding discretionary purchases with newly created money from underutilised resources instead of touching savings, income, or debt.*

### Case study

**Business.** His own purchase, not a client teardown: the Acquisition.com HQ building - roughly 36,000 sq ft - bought mainly so he could have a home gym and a venue for meetups and portfolio-company offsites.

**Starting state.** The building was not needed; it was wanted. Portfolio companies were already spending about $4 million a year on external event spaces, and his wife suggested a ~5,000 sq ft building as the appropriately-sized option for where they were at the time.

**Diagnosis.** The problem was not the price, it was the funding source. He framed the real risk as using money he would rather use elsewhere, and the correct fix as finding something the building itself could generate to pay for it.

**Intervention.**

- Buy the bigger building anyway, on the explicit condition that it must make more money than it costs.
- Look for a way to use existing underutilised resources ('sawdust money') rather than savings, income, or debt.
- Spin up advisory services, using the building and the portfolio as the asset, so the building generates its own income - explicitly described as fulfilling the promise made to Leila.

**Result.** No revenue figure is reported. He states the promise was that the building would make more money than it cost, and that spinning up advisory services was him keeping that promise.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| annual portfolio spend on external event spaces that the building was meant to displace | **$4,000,000/year** |
| size of the building bought | **36,000 sq ft** |
| size of the building his wife suggested | **5,000 sq ft** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Fund the discretionary purchase with newly created money from an asset you already underutilise, not with savings, income, or debt - and attach a defined payback window (he used one year) so the purchase has to earn its own keep. The desire is allowed; the funding source is the discipline.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- There is no client teardown; the case_study is his own building purchase and it has no reported revenue outcome, only a promise and the creation of advisory services. Any summary that presents this as a client case with results is wrong.
- The transcript contains two of the same story beats as other Hormozi material - 'sawdust' here means excess capacity monetised against a purchase, while in the delivery cube it means excess capacity monetised as a new product line; the two uses are not distinguished.
- The four money categories (past/income/debt/new) are presented as 'four ways to buy anything' but the 'new money' behaviour is really the only one taught; the first three are only defined so they can be ruled out.

## watch this if you're tired of being broke
`YFA8AS5Cu2w` · https://youtu.be/YFA8AS5Cu2w

*A three-step prescription for one specific broke viewer (Avante, two jobs, a one-year-old): cut every cost down to food and shelter, convert time into a higher-paying skill and keep trading up, and run volume until luck stops being a factor.*

### Case study

**Business.** Not a company teardown. Avante, a specific young man who stopped Hormozi in a grocery store: working two jobs with a one-year-old, who said he was sick and tired of being poor and asked how to get ahead.

**Starting state.** Two jobs and a one-year-old; Hormozi assumes the worst case of minimum wage at both jobs and 80 hours a week. No capital, no sellable skill, and (observed) spending on relatively nice clothes while struggling with money.

**Diagnosis.** He is trading the only asset he has - time - with low skills, which is the worst trade available. The second constraint is environmental: his information diet comes from people who are also poor, so their advice on money is reliably wrong for him.

**Intervention.**

- Cut all costs down to food and shelter only: no eating out for anything, discount grocery stores only, reuse/trade/Goodwill for clothing for two years, live with family or split with another family as cheaply as possible.
- Increase income: apply to at-home phone sales jobs whose starter roles need zero experience and pay $40,000+/year, working the existing job in between; drive Uber if he has a car, otherwise save to buy one.
- Sell someone else's stuff first, then learn to buy cheap and flip - cards, then furniture, then homes - trading up repeatedly.
- Set a $5 timer for 4 hours a day of study on exactly one chosen skill, stopping the timer whenever he looks away, until 20 hours of real work is done.
- Then convert those 4 hours into being the best applicant in the world: personalised messages to 4 people per company across 5 companies a day plus 10 cover letters, applying to ~1,000 places over 6 months, showing up in person after shifts.
- Once hired, outwork the top performer for one to two years rather than matching him, following the Kobe three-practices-a-day model.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| pay of the zero-experience sales roles he targets | **$40,000/year or more** |
| cash car budget | **$5,000-$10,000** |
| hours he assumes Avante already works per week | **80 hours** |
| time box for escaping the situation | **36 months** |

> **Transferable pattern.** With no capital and no skills, the bottleneck is not the business idea - it is converting time into a sellable skill and then into progressively more expensive inventory. Cut costs to the bone first so the time exists, put a hard number and a hard time box on everything (20 hours of study, 1,000 applications over 6 months, 36 months total), and outwork the incumbent rather than matching him.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The video is addressed to one named person (Avante) and contains no business and no outcome; case_study.result is null because none is reported. The 'case' is a person's situation, not a company.
- Framework summaries treat 'volume negates luck' as a mindset slogan; here it comes with explicit volume targets (1,000 applications / 6 months, 20 messages a day, 20 hours of study, 4 hours a day) that the slogan alone loses.
- The caption garbles the price of his own first car as 'A5 or $6,000' - the figure is recorded as stated rather than repaired.
- He recommends sales as the entry skill but the transcript never says what to sell inside that job; the selling ladder (cards to furniture to homes) is a separate, non-employment track.

## I Blew Up a Business Through 3 Small Changes (Just Copy Me)
`3yAiVjcImQ4` · https://youtu.be/3yAiVjcImQ4

*A music attorney losing $100,000 a year gets three fixes - kill the money-losing software and course side projects, route the YouTube audience deliberately into Instagram DMs, and replace $250/hour billing with a $5,800 flat fee plus commission anchored by a $25,000 offer - with a BANT-qualified CLOSER sales process underneath.*

### Case study

**Business.** A music attorney (a solo/small legal practice serving musicians) whose clients come to him for a specific result - e.g. getting IP protection in place so their music can be sold to a record label.

**Starting state.** Losing $100,000 a year. Billing $250/hour with an average client value of $1,500, i.e. about 6 hours per client. Spending the majority of his time on courses and software built to 'help everyone', with the software alone losing money, while the services business - the actual cash cow - was underinvested. Leads arrived ad hoc from Instagram DMs that nothing in his content pointed to; calls were booked ad hoc through Calendly or not at all; every call was run as a paid $250 legal consultation.

**Diagnosis.** Three stacked problems: (1) the help-everyone trap - unprofitable side projects consuming the hours that should have gone to scaling the cash cow, driven by an inability to focus and say no; (2) broken traffic - leads coming from a channel he never directed anyone to, with no CTA anywhere, so he was optimising the wrong thing and leaving $20-50k/month on the table; (3) an hourly billing trap - selling time instead of the result, which commoditised him and underpriced the outcome. Underneath all three, no repeatable sales process: no qualification, no script, no VSSL.

**Intervention.**

- Killed the vampire: shut down the money-losing software and the 'help everyone' side projects, and put the hours back into the services business.
- Repositioned the very cheap education as free education, turning it into a front end that ascends people into paid services and spreads by word of mouth.
- Doubled down on services by repricing for the best avatar rather than averaging A, B and C clients - he saw an easy double or triple available for the right ICP.
- Added CTAs at the 30% mark of YouTube videos driving viewers to Instagram to DM him.
- Put the same CTA in more places: video description, pinned comment, and the YouTube profile itself.
- Started proactively DMing new followers - most arrived from YouTube - opening with 'here for free stuff or do you want help with your legal stuff?', which triaged qualified leads up front.
- Ditched hourly billing: $5,800 upfront flat fee plus a commission when he closes a deal for the client (some deals worth several hundred thousand).
- Added a $25,000 zero-commission B offer as an anchor so the $5,800 core offer reads as a steal.
- Added a hands-off downsell at $2,000-$3,000 for unqualified buyers, deliberately close enough to the core offer that the core offer is the obvious path.
- Built a real sales motion: a 5-7 minute VSSL, BANT qualification, a scripted consultation (not a consultation - a sales call) using CLOSER and the plus-minus-minus-plus structure, and call recordings reviewed for continuous improvement.

**Result.** No single closing revenue figure is given. Reported outcomes: the $100,000/year loss was the starting state; the price went from $250/hour to $5,800 upfront plus commission; traffic fixes were estimated to recover $20-50k/month that was already being generated but not routed. He notes the business was at stage four ('prioritize') of the scaling roadmap with 'product' as the constraint, and that the fix pattern (specialized product, V2 price to serve the new niche avatar, better free stuff, more…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| annual loss before intervention | **$100,000/year** |
| hourly rate before | **$250/hour** |
| average client value before | **$1,500 (about 6 hours)** |
| new core price | **$5,800 upfront plus commission** |
| anchor B offer | **$25,000 with zero commission** |
| downsell price | **$2,000-$3,000** |
| monthly revenue left on the table from unoptimised traffic | **$20,000-$50,000/month** |
| CTA placement in YouTube videos | **30% mark** |
| VSSL length | **5 to 7 minutes** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Fix the three leaks in order: (1) kill whatever is losing money and eating the founder's hours, then push those hours into the one thing that already works; (2) find where customers already arrive by accident and put deliberate CTAs there - plus DM the followers you already have, opening with a two-option triage question ('free stuff or help?'); (3) replace time-based pricing with a flat fee priced against the result, and anchor it with a much higher zero-commission B offer and a slightly-cheaper DIY downsell so the core offer is obviously the best path. An exceptionally high close rate is…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The video is structured around three problems, but the fourth (no sales process) is introduced as 'the fourth problem that came up' inside the same teardown and is arguably the largest intervention - summaries that count only three changes understate the work.
- No end-state revenue is reported for the attorney. The only hard before-numbers are the $100,000/year loss, $250/hour, $1,500 average client value; the after-numbers are prices set, not revenue achieved.
- The transcript contains roughly two minutes of book-launch advertising ('$100 million Money Models', August 16th event, mystery headliners) spliced into the middle of the teardown - any extraction that treats those numbers as business claims is wrong.
- The down sell is described as something he is 'not always a big fan of' and was only added because the attorney had so many unqualified customers - the standard framing of downsells as universally good loses that caveat.

## "I'm Broke, What Business Do I Start?"
`nIk3DedjxJM` · https://youtu.be/nIk3DedjxJM

*A five-step process for finding what to sell from nothing - the three Ps (pain, profession, passion), narrowing the who to at least three frames, describing the good stuff and the bad stuff in the customer's own words, assembling it into one sentence, then naming a unique mechanism - plus a four-hour-a-day outreach routine to get the first five customers.*

### Case study

**Business.** A registered dietitian who left a hospital job and now teaches other registered dietitians how to bill insurance - a business built from the Profession P.

**Starting state.** Working as an RD in a hospital six days a week, 12+ hours a day, leaving her only one day a week to bill her own personal clients on the side. That constraint forced her to figure out a complex insurance billing system and do it fast. At the time of the video she has 5,800 Instagram followers.

**Diagnosis.** The valuable asset was not the dietetics knowledge, it was the billing workaround she had been forced to invent. The narrowness of the problem is the point - it did not need to be a big idea.

**Intervention.**

- Took the specific thing she learned from her profession - how to bill insurance quickly as an RD - rather than the profession itself.
- Made a business around something very narrow: teaching other registered dietitians that same billing process.
- Built the audience on Instagram rather than needing a large following anywhere.

**Result.** She takes home almost a million dollars a year in income from a 5,800-follower Instagram account. No timeframe or revenue-vs-income breakdown is given.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| hospital workload before the business | **6 days a week, 12+ hours per day** |
| Instagram following | **5,800** |
| annual income | **almost $1,000,000** |

> **Transferable pattern.** The business comes from the workaround you were forced to invent, not from the job title. Take the narrowest specific process you had to figure out under pressure, and sell that process to the other people who have the same job and the same constraint - a 5,800-follower account was enough because the niche was narrow enough to command the price.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The video is a five-step framework with embedded examples, not a teardown; the case_study emitted here is the dietitian anecdote, which is the only business in the transcript with a starting state, a diagnosis and a result. It is two sentences of source material.
- The four-rung pricing ladder ($19 / $199 / $1,999 / $10,000) is the same offer narrowed four times - any summary that presents these as four different products' prices has misread it.
- The value equation is taught here as 'the four elements of the value equation but written in the positive' (easy, guaranteed, immediate, exactly what they want) with the negative framing as the inverse - the standard framing presents only the positive side.
- The 'three-letter method' is just A-S-K; the naming implies more than the content delivers.
- One out of two people making their first dollar is a platform statistic for paid communities on school, not a general business-success rate.

## Can I Save This Failing Theme Park in 90 Days?
`xRxVpjeHmeA` · https://youtu.be/xRxVpjeHmeA

*A cash-constrained indoor adventure park that has burned $22M and is weeks from death gets a single bet: a 7-10 day summer-camp giveaway that floods the list with leads, converts via phone, and buys the business another quarter - then repeat the same play for birthdays.*

### Case study

**Business.** Boulder Adventure Park - an indoor family entertainment centre in Grand Prairie, Texas, founded by Paul Fontinelli, who left corporate America eight years ago with three young kids. Revenue streams: general admission plus in-park spend (arcade, food and beverage, merchandise) making up about 70%, and group business (church groups, social groups, summer camps).

**Starting state.** Total build cost $22M, of which $8M was raised and the rest bank debt. Revenue running at '4.8' against a stated goal of $10M. Break-even nut is about $550,000/month; actual is about $400,000/month; monthly debt service is about $180,000/month. Cash-constrained since opening - at the point of filming the owner had been told he was 14 days from not making payroll, and had already put his entire 401k in. Peak day runs at only 50% of capacity. Sales team: 3 people. Total headcount: 150, of whom…

**Diagnosis.** Demand-constrained, not capacity-constrained - the capacity exists and is half empty. But the binding constraint is cash, so the only intervention worth doing is one that generates cash inside the 90-day window. The owner was tracking outputs (revenue) instead of the inputs (LTV, CAC) that produce them. The summer camp window was open right then - malls book summer programmes in May-August - and the business only had one shot at getting the offer right. Hormozi also flags the owner's three-person sales team as the limit on what lead volume could actually be converted.

**Intervention.**

- Drop the season pass idea and bet on summer instead - one bet only, because there was no luxury of time.
- Keep the existing summer camp structure ($300 for 3 days/week, $500 for 5, $2,000 for any day all summer) but reframe it as 'buy four, get ten' and 'buy one month, get the whole summer', adding 'early bird' as the reason for the offer.
- Build a giveaway as the front end: first prize a free full-summer private camp experience; second prize $3,000 off the $5,000 notional value, which lands exactly on the $2,000 core ticket. More than one second-place winner for compliance.
- Add a referral mechanic on the thank-you page - forward the page, each opt-in earns an extra drawing entry, and the referrer wins too if their referral wins.
- Fix the landing page: strip the extra banners to one, remove the header that adds no value, put trust next to the action (parent rating near the button), add an obvious safety stat ('last year zero falls'), add a day-one money-back guarantee, and lead with a VSSL at the top.
- Run it as a 7-10 day campaign with a countdown timer, pushing both the email list and paid ads, and daily email/text reminders of days left.
- On drawing day, call the winner, then call every other entrant as a second-place winner with a 72-hour claim window ('our summer camp's filling up').
- Sell the leads on the phone using the standard offer, then flip the campaign to the evergreen 'buy four get six' structure for the rest of the summer.
- Record a VSSL - which turned out to be the single best-performing asset on the page and the best-converting ad creative too.
- After the campaign, repeat the identical play for birthdays at a $2,000-$3,000 budget and hire salespeople to handle the volume.

**Result.** 3,700 leads in a local market (about 120/day), with between a third and half arriving in the final 48 hours. Summer camp revenue up 325% versus prior year. Admissions doubled over four to six weeks once Hormozi's own video clips were used as ads. But the close rate suffered: the three-person sales team could not call the leads fast enough, and Paul says the result could have been much higher with proper manpower and a call sequence. Hormozi's verdict: the intervention bought Paul roughly three…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| total capital sunk | **$22,000,000** |
| break-even monthly revenue | **$550,000/month** |
| current monthly revenue | **$400,000/month** |
| monthly debt service | **about $180,000/month** |
| days until cash ran out | **14 days** |
| cash the play needed to generate before the slow season | **$600,000** |
| leads generated | **3,700** |
| summer camp revenue increase vs prior year | **325%** |
| admissions increase after running Hormozi clips as ads | **doubled over 4-6 weeks** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When a business is weeks from death, do not fix the business - buy time. Pick the single highest-cash offer available inside the current seasonal window, run it as a short prize-led giveaway with a hard countdown and a 72-hour claim window, and make sure the second-place prize lands exactly on your core paid offer so the giveaway pre-sells it. Model the final 48 hours as a third to a half of all leads regardless of campaign length. Then repeat the identical play in a cheaper, year-round version (here: birthdays) - and fix the sales capacity before the leads arrive, because in this teardown…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The video's own framing is 'fix the business', but the intervention only buys time - Hormozi states outright that it bought three more months to live. Any summary that reports this as a turnaround overstates it.
- The offer that produced the result (summer camp giveaway) was not the offer Hormozi originally proposed (a season pass). He switched after Paul surfaced the summer camp window; summaries that credit the season pass are wrong.
- The single biggest failure in the teardown is not in the framework at all: the sales team was too small to call 3,700 leads, and Paul says the outcome could have been much higher. The intervention list Hormozi gives does not include fixing sales capacity until the follow-up conversation.
- Paul's revenue is stated as '4.8' with no unit, and the goal as '10 million revenue'; the transcript never confirms the unit of 4.8 and this extraction records it as stated.
- The caption garbles the general admission price as '$3246 per person' (almost certainly $32-$46); it is omitted rather than repaired. The $11 in-park spend is clean and recorded.

## Helping a Stranger Build A $15,000,000/yr Business in 32 Minutes
`B-ogfFiQpXg` · https://youtu.be/B-ogfFiQpXg

*A $3M concierge medicine practice in Sarasota gets an event-based demand engine instead of a call funnel: big giveaway at events, everyone gets a scan, they watch a VSSL while being scanned, then close - plus a 'who do you want to bring with you' referral mechanic attached to every single patient touchpoint.*

### Case study

**Business.** Precision Health Concierge Medicine - a concierge/optimisation medical practice in Sarasota, Florida, owned by Dr. Zad Oasi (CEO), with a founding partner as medical director. Members pay an annual fee; revenue is augmented by aesthetics treatments, supplementation, and an expensive body scan. The practice is 16 people.

**Starting state.** Bought 18 months before filming; the business had traded 18 years. Revenue was about $1.8M at purchase, grown to $3M in the last 12 months, with $600K profit excluding the owner's ~$300K compensation. Three-year goal is $15M. Marketing was the stated bottleneck: word of mouth had recently been overtaken by SEO, after $50,000 spent on an agency that produced no progress (Hormozi refers to the same spend as $55,000). Lead flow: phone call handled by an in-house marketer, then a 15-minute slot on…

**Diagnosis.** Marketing is the constraint, but the wrong shape of marketing. Hormozi classifies the existing process as warm, not cold - a $10K/year purchase after a phone call and a 15-minute physician slot only works because buyers already know the practice. That means paid cold traffic is not the immediate play. The referrals already happening were not being lubricated: a $500 credit makes no difference to members paying $5K, so the referral offer was social-capital neutral instead of positive. And the newsletter had no call to action at all. He also names the sector-wide failure mode: physicians…

**Intervention.**

- Speed up the referral machine with a referral-specific offer instead of a cash credit: a $1,000-$2,000 ticket treatment given to the friend (or to both), only available to referrals, so the referral becomes a gift rather than a discount.
- Give members five of those treatments - one per visit on the $5K membership - and ask 'who do you want to bring with you?' at every single treatment, reframed as a benefit of membership rather than a referral request.
- Anchor the referral request at the 90-day point, where patients reliably report feeling the change.
- Add a PS call to action to the newsletter running a quarterly drawing to win a year of the premium VIP service, with everyone who enters receiving something regardless.
- Give away a year of the VIP service (a $20K value) as the grand prize at events, so the price can be stated without sticker shock and everyone else can be offered the $5K/$10K tiers afterwards.
- Move demand generation to events: run one per week, sponsor or host where high-net-worth older clients already gather. At the event, everyone gets a scan; while being scanned (a 20-minute window) they watch a VSSL, then close immediately afterwards. V2 of the test inserts a follow-up appointment…
- Second, more scalable version: a one-day workshop marketed with Meta ads, charged at $99 to get a small commitment and a card on file, with the $500 scan included; then book in-person closes with a VSSL beforehand.
- Keep the existing sales process untouched - the diagnosis was that it works for warm traffic.

**Result.** No revenue result is reported inside the session. Hormozi's model: a 300-person event yields scans on a third (~100 scans), 25% conversion yields 25 sales, which at the practice's LTV is about a $2.5M event - and he sets a target of $200,000-$400,000 from 10 events in one quarter, which would pace the practice to $10M+ by year end. He predicts this will be the business of those he looked at that generates the most money in the shortest time, and rates it 'scaling'. The owner's own 90-day update…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| revenue at purchase | **$1,800,000** |
| revenue after 12 months | **$3,000,000** |
| profit excluding owner comp | **$600,000** |
| three-year revenue goal | **$15,000,000** |
| modelled LTV of a single well-run event | **$2,500,000** |
| patient count | **475** |
| headcount | **16** |

> **Transferable pattern.** For a high-trust, high-ticket service, do not start with cold paid traffic - classify your process as warm or cold first. Then attach the referral request to the touchpoints that already exist (at the close, and at every treatment) and reframe it from 'refer a friend' to 'who do you want to bring with you?', backed by a perk with real face value that is only available to referrals. Finally, if you have an expensive diagnostic or assessment, use it as the sales window itself: run the video sales letter while the customer is being scanned, and close the moment it ends.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The manifest title says $15,000,000/yr; that is the owner's three-year goal, not a current or achieved figure. The practice is at $3M.
- The intervention is not tested within the video - no result is reported. The only follow-up is the owner's own admission that he did not run the event play because of Sarasota seasonality, so this teardown's recommendations remain unverified in the source.
- The failed-agency spend is stated as $50,000 by the owner and $55,000 by Hormozi in the same conversation; both figures are recorded rather than reconciled.
- Hormozi explicitly says the existing sales process should not be touched - a summary that lists 'fix the sales process' as part of this teardown would be contradicting the transcript.
- The video comes from a competition format ('Scale or Fail', 8 owners, $100,000 prize), and Hormozi says this business is the one he thinks can generate the most money fastest - a judgement, not a measured outcome.

## Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes
`OQf2Ba-Lp_4` · https://youtu.be/OQf2Ba-Lp_4

*A $1.25M HVAC duct-cleaning business with 38% margins and an 82% close rate gets a 10% price rise (worth ~25% more net profit), an ads landing page built as a standalone funnel page, an IOU/reactivation email campaign, and an affiliate offer where partners keep 100% of a $175 lead-magnet sale - plus proof a year later that revenue nearly doubled.*

### Case study

**Business.** Proshine Professional Cleaning - an HVAC cleaning and duct work repair company in the Hilton Head / Bluffton area, run by Corey and his wife Nicole. Core services: HVAC duct cleaning at $1,575/unit with a 2-year growth-free guarantee, duct work re-wrapping, and dryer vent cleaning at $175. A large share of business comes from affiliate referrals from HVAC, pest control and remediation companies.

**Starting state.** Trailing 12-month revenue $1.25M, profit $479,000, net margin 38%. $60,000 of debt, with about 10% of profit allocated to paying it down, planned to clear in four to five months. Show rate 99%, close rate 82%. Marketing spend just under $7,200/month; 60% of customers from paid ads ($3,000/month Google, just raised to $5,000; $650/month Facebook, two weeks old), 15% from third-party local SEO, and a substantial share from affiliates - one HVAC partner alone sends about $30,000/month, and Corey…

**Diagnosis.** Demand-constrained, not supply-constrained - he could handle a doubling of lead flow, which means the whole game is lead throughput, not capacity. There was nothing majorly wrong: 38% margins and an 82% close rate. So this is incremental improvement, not a Hail Mary. The specific leaks: (1) the business was underpriced - an 80%+ close rate is the tell; (2) Google ads were landing on the home page and then requiring another click to an offer page, i.e. two landing pages in a row, losing roughly half the traffic; (3) the Facebook creative was unreadable at mobile size with the offer buried…

**Intervention.**

- Raise prices 10% - to about $1,650 per unit - on the condition that the close rate stays above 65%, which at a 38% margin is worth roughly 25% more net profit, about $100,000+/year at last year's volume.
- Keep paying the $60,000 debt down on the existing four-to-five-month schedule (Hormozi's view: debt increases risk, and risk comes due over long horizons).
- Build a dedicated ads landing page separate from the home page: single-line mobile header with just the phone number, hamburger menu, headline, free 18-point inspection offer, form, phone number, locations and FAQs - and redirect every button on the main site to it.
- Fix the ads: 40 variations across brand colours, drop the text to an offer-first headline, put the local area in the copy ('Hilton Head Bluffton'), make the free 18-point inspection the visual hero, and use photos of technicians with smiling customers rather than photos blocking the work.
- Repurpose the best-performing organic posts as ads by tacking a 5-second call to action onto the back - the algorithm has already done the testing for you.
- Increase ad spend only after the funnel and the ads are fixed, because fixing those two may double or triple lead flow without spending more.
- Add cross-platform retargeting (item seven) and bid on every branded search term permutation (item eight).
- Run a reactivation email campaign once a month, structured as three mini-campaigns rather than six individual emails: an IOU / 'we messed up' email with a follow-up, an allergies angle (pollen in April, mildew smell when heating kicks in) with case studies as the follow-up, and a savings angle…
- Build a real affiliate programme with an offer attached: partners sell the $175 dryer vent clean and keep 100% of it, Corey does the work. Effective CAC is the $25 delivery cost divided by the upsell rate - about $75 per customer at one in three.
- Go outbound to HOAs with a calendar-building approach: one to two events per week, and book the next event before leaving each one.
- Pick ONE of the two affiliate motions (events vs partner offers) rather than both, and staff it with someone full-time - which makes it a 2026 project.

**Result.** One-year check-in: revenue moved from $1.25M trailing to a $2.3M-$2.5M run rate, with Hormozi summarising it as 'almost doubled within a year'. Lead flow went from about 120/month to about 200/month, with higher quality leads. Corey attributes the biggest impact to marketing: they replaced the third-party agency with one that had done it for other companies, and made the landing page conversions, marketing changes and ad spend increases. He is planning another location in the next 12 months.…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| revenue at first profiling | **$1,250,000 trailing 12 months** |
| profit | **$479,000** |
| net margin | **38%** |
| debt | **$60,000** |
| close rate at first profiling | **82%** |
| show rate | **99%** |
| price raise recommended | **10%, to ~$1,650/unit** |
| close-rate floor for the raise to pay off | **65%** |
| profit impact of the raise | **~25% more net profit, ~$100,000+/year** |
| current ROAS on the unoptimised page | **13:1** |
| revenue one year later | **$2.3M-$2.5M run rate** |
| leads per month before and after | **~120 -> ~200** |

> **Transferable pattern.** With a healthy, high-margin business the move is incremental, not a rebuild: raise price to the point where the close rate would have to fall below a stated floor for it to lose money (an 80%+ close rate is the signal), then fix the funnel and the creative BEFORE adding spend, because a page that converts and ads that read at mobile size may multiply lead flow for free. Then stack the compounding layers in order: retargeting, your own branded search terms, a reactivation email campaign framed as 'we owe you' rather than 'we're back', and finally a real affiliate programme where the partner…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The video is titled '$2,500,000' and the business reached a $2.3-2.5M run rate - but that is a run rate at the check-in, not a trailing-twelve-month figure, and Hormozi describes it only as 'almost doubled'.
- The plan's projections are stated as independent multiples (2x pages, 2-3x ads, 10-20% retargeting, 20-30% email, 25% profit) and are not additive in the transcript - any summary that totals them is inventing a number.
- The affiliate programme Hormozi designed was never implemented within the timeframe of the video - he explicitly schedules it as a 2026 project needing a full-time owner, so it is untested here.
- The single largest factor in the actual result may be the agency replacement Corey describes at the check-in ('went with a new third party that's been there, done that'), which was not part of Hormozi's plan at all.
- The 33% allergy-reduction and 90%-of-houses stats are ad angles Hormozi suggests, not verified figures - the transcript does not attribute them to a source.
