## Building a $5,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 42 Mins
`sBJppqCeFGI` · https://youtu.be/sBJppqCeFGI

*A six-location chiropractic chain doing $5.2M at 23% net gets told its close rate is too high (71% vs a 30-40% healthy band), its Google ROAS of 12:1-24:1 is massively under-spent, and its real problem is that it sells at the point of greatest satisfaction instead of greatest pain - plus a $29 credit-card lead magnet, pre-loaded insurance verification, and a four-step same-day sale.*

### Case study

**Business.** ChiroFirst of Washington (as stated in the caption - 'Kyo first of Washington'), a six-location chiropractic chain founded by Raymond Coer. Services: custom treatment plans of chiropractic, rehab and spinal decompression over 60-90 days, with spinal decompression as the differentiator. 75% insurance, 25% cash. All six locations were acquired rather than opened organically.

**Starting state.** Trailing 12-month revenue $5.2M, EBITDA roughly $1.2M, net margin about 23%. On a single location: 35 leads/month, 28 show (80% show rate), 71% close, roughly 20 sales/month. CAC about $700, LTV $3,400 (4.8:1). Marketing spend $1,500-$2,000 per location per month ($1,000 Facebook, $500-$1,000 Google), about $110,000/year in total. Google ROAS across three clinics was 12:1, 24:1 and 9:1; the Kent clinic ran an 8:1 Facebook ROAS with a CAC half of Capitol Hill's. Core packages $2,400-$3,600; 1 in…

**Diagnosis.** Three findings, none of them about strategy. (1) The close rate is too high: at 71% against a healthy band of 30-40%, the market is willing to pay more, and the price points themselves are already right (packages, not per-visit). (2) The Google channel is drastically under-spent - a machine that returns $24 for every $1 in, with the owner spending only $500-$1,000/month per location because a third-party agency recommended it. (3) The clinic sells at the point of greatest satisfaction rather than greatest pain: it relieves the pain with a light treatment on day one and only presents the paid…

**Intervention.**

- Increase Google spend as the first move - double it and add more keywords - because the measured return is 9:1 to 24:1 and the channel is the highest-intent traffic available.
- Add a front-end lead magnet: a $19-$29 first consult or x-ray (or $29 x-ray plus assessment) taken over the phone so a credit card is captured, purely to drive show rates to essentially 100%.
- Tighten the ad copy: combine the call out into one line ('Attention Everett residents with back pain'), lead with a question or the offer rather than proof, put the offer in the headline, compress the body into a handful of bullets, and state scarcity ('we can only see 10 new patients per week').
- Capture the credit card AND the insurance card on the phone at booking, and have the front desk print the insurance packets the morning of, so the doctor walks in with a completed template.
- Reorder the same-day sale: take the assessment, then sell the package, then deliver the first treatment (or have them come back) - selling before relief rather than after. Projected 10-15% immediate sales boost plus a higher close rate.
- Build the prescriptive close: turn the top-performing doctor's approach into a visual aid (a laptop turned to the patient, or a clipboard script the doctor ticks through) so the process is identical at every location and every patient gets the same pitch.
- Apply document/demonstrate/duplicate: the owner documents the checklist, demonstrates it, and has staff duplicate it in front of him.
- Have the sales manager take over the sales process at one location as a test before rolling it out.
- Add local SEO on long-tail local keywords ('chiropractor Everett', 'spine Everett', 'sciatic'), ranking each market individually so new locations inherit the playbook.
- Talk to the ad agency in marketer language: give them a target CPA/CPL with a little padding above the number he is actually willing to pay, and tell them to spend up to it.

**Result.** No result is reported inside the session - the video ends with the plan. Hormozi's projections: an easy 2x in lead flow from the ad copy and lead magnet changes; plus 10% from reordering the same-day sale; local SEO worth 30-50% but taking about a year; and about a 20% lift from the sales process changes. He estimates that doubling revenue across the existing locations would already put the business at $5M EBITDA without opening another store, since fixed costs stay roughly the same. Total…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| revenue | **$5,200,000 trailing 12 months** |
| EBITDA and net margin | **~$1,200,000 at 23%** |
| close rate | **71%** |
| show rate | **80%** |
| CAC and LTV | **$700 CAC, $3,400 LTV, 4.8:1** |
| Google ROAS across three clinics | **12:1, 24:1, 9:1** |
| Kent clinic Facebook ROAS | **8:1, lowest CAC by a decent margin** |
| package prices | **$2,400-$3,600** |
| projected revenue doubling effect | **$5M EBITDA if revenue doubled** |
| implementation time | **about 6 months** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When the same model produces different results at different locations, the lever is the people, not the model - so pick interventions with low operational risk. Then look for the two signs that money is being left on the table: a close rate far above the healthy 30-40% band (you are underpriced) and a measured ROAS of 10:1 or better on a channel you are barely funding (you are under-spent; efficiency will fall as you scale and that is fine, down to about a 5:1 floor). Finally, check WHEN you ask for the sale: if you relieve the pain before you present the price, you are selling at the point…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- No result is reported - the video ends at the plan, and unlike other teardowns in this batch there is no 90-day or 1-year check-in. All outcomes are projections.
- The 71% close rate is measured at one location, and the transcript never gives a chain-wide close rate; the healthy 30-40% band is Hormozi's general rule of thumb, not a benchmark for this business.
- The projections (2x lead flow, +10%, 30-50% SEO, 20% sales lift) are stated separately and are not additive in the transcript.
- The video's stated goal is a $5M EBITDA three-year target, but the illustration of 'doubling revenue puts you at five' is revenue, not EBITDA - the two $5M figures are different measures and are easy to conflate.
- The business name appears in the caption only as 'Kyo first of Washington', which is a mis-transcription; it is recorded as stated rather than repaired.

His…

## Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 57 Mins
`n6SHLmKcY0E` · https://youtu.be/n6SHLmKcY0E

*A cocktail consultancy with $1.1M revenue, an $11,800 CAC and a 20% upsell rate is told to stop selling $30,000 to strangers: build a $5,800 pricing-audit front end that pays for itself, put a lead magnet between cold traffic and the sale, and let the founder sell one-call closes instead of three-call closes.*

### Case study

**Business.** Unfiltered Hospitality - a bar and beverage program consultancy co-founded by Ben (ex-investment banker, ex-bar owner) and his business partner Ghee. Clients are restaurants, hotels, bars, country clubs, cruise ships and nightclubs. Two products: 'better cocktail consulting' (phase one, 90 days - design the cocktail menu, train the team, install the operating system) and the 'program performance retainer' (phase two - weekly KPI scorecard call, seasonal monthly cocktails, quarterly 2-day…

**Starting state.** 2024 revenue $1.1M, net profit $123,000 (about 11.3% net margin), 4.5 years in business, over 200 bars helped. Core offer priced at $30,000, sold as a straight call funnel. CAC $12,000 (restated as $11,800 in the recap) against an LTV:CAC of 1.7:1. Marketing spend excluding salaries $10,000/month. Close rate 66. Fewer than 20% of core-offer buyers take the retainer upsell, and those who do churn after two quarters. Revenue is unstable - weeks with no leads at all followed by good months - which…

**Diagnosis.** An offer problem, which Hormozi says is strategic because changing the offer changes the advertising, the conversion process, the pricing and the deliverables. Specifically: a $30,000 engagement is being sold cold, on a straight call funnel, to people who have never met him - 'the right offer at the wrong time is still the wrong offer'. The $12,000 CAC is the evidence, since a customer like this should cost $1,500-$2,500. There is no lead magnet between cold traffic and the sale, so low trust is being asked to jump straight to a sale. The avatar is too broad. The funnel has bad friction…

**Intervention.**

- Narrow the avatar to operational restaurants and bars doing $4M+/year in revenue - owners who think about the business rather than about a passion project - and put the qualification directly in the ads and on the funnel ('for $4 million plus only').
- Rewrite the ad call outs to name the avatar in the first line, replace the business name with the avatar, and add a pain-based hook (e.g. cocktails under 10% of revenue year over year, no good post about your cocktails in two years, your cocktail programme is flaccid) - because describing the pain…
- Move from feature-driven to benefit/experience-driven copy: describe the moments (customers excited to open the menu and ordering two or three times more; no more disaster back bar) rather than processes and data.
- Build a lead magnet - top 10 worst drinks to serve and how to replace them - and split test it against the existing profit-calculator tool rather than stacking them; track all the way through LTV, not just opt-ins, because the $97 vs $47 test showed identical conversion at double the price with…
- Rebuild the funnel: strip the logo and the 'better bar program' line from above the fold, make the headline the promise, make the subheadline the single largest objection to that promise, and reduce the first page to headline, subheadline, image, opt-in.
- Move the video off YouTube to a third-party host, and place a VSSL above the scheduler on the booking page plus a second VSSL and the lead magnet on the post-booking page, so the pitch is delivered perfectly every time and the human call starts at 'how's everything sound?'.
- Fix the duplicate data entry (bad friction) while keeping qualification (good friction).
- Replace the $30,000 cold sale with a $5,800 front end - a pricing audit/booster that solves one specific problem very well and produces roughly a $50,000 ROI - sold as a one-call close rather than a three-call close.
- Sell the $5,800 on the phone as a discovery call, then deliver it fast (about a 30-day fix), and use a rollover upsell to credit the $5,800 toward the year of the full programme - preferring to spread the discount at $1,500 off per quarter rather than cutting the first payment to $4,000.
- Make the rollover offer inside the 30-day window at three moments: the milestone moment when the first weekend's sales land, the following week, and last chance.
- Add a waived-fee AB close for the back end: $30,000, waived if they commit for a year, but owed if they cancel two quarters in - 'I take the risk on, you make the commitment'.
- Add an ultra-high-ticket option at 5x the price where Ben delivers personally, presented first so the team-delivered version reads as the value choice.
- Fix churn before scaling: get login access to the client's systems and show them their numbers monthly (about 2 hours per account), so the value is demonstrated rather than requested.
- Have Ben take all sales calls personally until he physically cannot, with a set agenda: the director of ops books the call and tells them to watch the video first, and the first question on the call is 'did you watch the video?'.
- Only increase ad spend after the funnel and offer are fixed - and when testing, budget 2x the 30-day cash collected per campaign before shutting an ad off.

**Result.** No outcome is reported - the video ends at the plan. Hormozi's projections, stated separately and not additive: the funnel redo alone could triple lead volume; ad call outs could 2-3x click-through; landing page conversion could go from 7% to about 30% (a 4x); close rate from 6% to 30-50%; upsell rate to at least 50% against today's less than 20%; and founder selling alone would be 'more than a 5x in sales'. At a 30% close rate he says Ben would make the same revenue on the front end alone,…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| revenue | **$1,100,000 (2024)** |
| net profit | **$123,000 at 11.3%** |
| CAC | **$12,000 (recapped as $11,800)** |
| the CAC this customer should cost | **$1,500-$2,500, up to $3,500** |
| core offer price | **$30,000** |
| upsell rate | **less than 20%** |
| new front-end price | **$5,800** |
| retainer price | **$9,000 per quarter** |
| landing page conversion | **about 7%, target about 30%** |
| projected sales multiple from founder selling | **more than 5x** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When a premium offer will not sell, check the timing before the price: a $30,000 engagement sold cold to strangers is the wrong offer at the wrong time, no matter how good it is. Insert a lead magnet between cold traffic and the sale to move people from low trust to high trust, then build a front-end offer at roughly a fifth of the price that solves one narrow problem so well it produces ten times its cost - and roll that payment into the back end rather than discounting it. Spread the rollover credit over four quarters, not the first payment, so you get commitment rather than an easy yes.…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- No result is reported - the video ends at the plan, and every figure after the starting state is a projection. Hormozi says explicitly these are 'high likely shots' and 'in no way a promise'.
- The projections (3x lead volume, 2-3x CTR, 4x landing page conversion, 30-50% close, 50%+ upsell, 5x sales) are stated separately and are not additive in the transcript.
- CAC is stated as $12,000 by Ben and restated as $11,800 in Hormozi's recap of the same numbers - both are recorded rather than reconciled.
- The churn problem (retainer customers stopping after two quarters) is the one issue Hormozi says must be fixed before anything else, but the intervention for it is a two-hour-per-month manual process rather than a structural fix, and he openly says the alternative is to accept the churn and price…
- The '10x their investment the first year, 30% increase in menu orders' figures are offered as ad copy examples, not as verified results for this business.
- The stated revenue goal is captioned as '3 million by the end of 2020', which cannot be correct given the 2024 figures - the year is a caption error and is recorded as stated.

## He Makes $600,000,000/Yr Selling Bacon
`orMbq2LtzKE` · https://youtu.be/orMbq2LtzKE

*The $18M-funded failure that came before ButcherBox: Mike Salguero buys CustomMade.com for $140,000, grows it from $35,000/year to $60,000/month, then raises on a 'marketplace' narrative he cannot deliver and loses the company, his team and his friends over eight years.*

### Case study

**Business.** CustomMade.com - a marketplace connecting customers to woodworkers and makers for custom pieces (custom coffee tables, custom jewellery). Bought in 2008 by Mike Salguero and his best friend Seth out of their real-estate jobs, and later repositioned as a venture-backed marketplace.

**Starting state.** Bought for $140,000 with a $2,500 deposit and 90 days of due diligence, which they used to raise money instead. The site had strong inbound traffic from its domain name but was badly run: makers paid $35/year and had to email the owner to upload content. Initial revenue was about $35,000/year. After a rebuild and a sales team calling makers for subscriptions, revenue reached about $60,000/month - roughly 12 months of strong growth - and the business was nearly profitable.

**Diagnosis.** The fatal error was strategic, not operational: they raised on a narrative. After failing to raise from VCs on the real business, Mike described the job board as a marketplace and 'as soon as I said the word marketplace, everyone wanted an interview' - so they raised $1.9M on a premise that was not the actual business. Once investors had bought the marketplace story, they could not pivot away from it, even when the model proved unworkable. The structural problem: a custom transaction requires 60 back-and-forth exchanges, and standing in the middle of that to take a 10% (effectively 7%) fee…

**Intervention.**

- Bought the business for $140,000 with a $2,500 deposit and 90 days of due diligence, and used the due-diligence window to raise $500,000.
- Overhauled the site so makers could log in and manage their own content, and raised subscription prices.
- Built a sales team to call makers and sell annual or monthly subscriptions, taking revenue from $35,000/year to about $60,000/month in roughly 12 months.
- Raised another $500,000, then pivoted the pitch to 'marketplace' to raise $1.9M at a $7M pre-money valuation (First Round Capital, Google Ventures).
- Six months later accepted $4M at $16M from an excluded VC, diluting further.
- Later raised $18M at a $30M valuation - structured as $10M equity, $4M debt, $4M secondary - allowing original investors to take 3x.
- Under investor pressure, fired the entire original team (tech, then product, then marketing) over about a year and replaced them with new hires with no written culture.
- Eventually did a friendly foreclosure with the venture-debt bank, handing the company over; the co-founder stayed on and converted it into a jewellery company with no marketplace.

**Result.** Failure. Eight years (2008-2015) with nothing to show: GMV peaked around $3-4M/month but take rate was about 7% (roughly $200,000/month) while burn at its height was $500,000/month. Mike's ownership was diluted to about 8% and he had 'a good salary' but no outcome. The company was foreclosed on by its venture-debt lender. 50 people were let go, and Mike let go of the friends who had built the company with him. He describes sitting in his car in the parking lot unable to go into the office. His…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| purchase price | **$140,000** |
| deposit paid | **$2,500** |
| revenue before the rebuild | **$35,000/year** |
| revenue after the rebuild | **about $60,000/month** |
| first institutional round | **$1,900,000 at $7,000,000 pre-money** |
| second round | **$4,000,000 at $16,000,000** |
| third round | **$18,000,000 at $30,000,000 ($10M equity, $4M debt, $4M…** |
| peak GMV | **about $3,000,000-$4,000,000/month** |
| take rate | **about 7% (nominally 10%)** |
| peak monthly burn | **$500,000/month** |
| founder ownership at the end | **about 8%** |
| duration | **8 years (2008-2015)** |
| people let go | **50** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Do not raise on a story that is not your actual business - once investors buy the narrative you can no longer pivot away from it, even when the model is unworkable. And model the unit economics of the middle: standing between two parties to take a fee only works if the transaction is simple, and here each sale required dozens of exchanges to earn a 7% cut. The counterfactual Mike and Hormozi both draw is that the bootstrapped version - $35,000/year to $60,000/month, nearly profitable - was the better business, and the capital destroyed it.

### Case study

**Business.** ButcherBox - a direct-to-consumer meat subscription shipping grass-fed beef, chicken, pork and seafood. Founded by Mike Salguero in September 2015, one weekend after closing CustomMade. Bootstrapped, profitable from day one, and still owning its own backbone only partially: no farms, no slaughterhouses, no distribution - the only owned piece is two dry-ice plants.

**Starting state.** Started as an intended hobby business (inspired by The 4-Hour Workweek), built on WordPress over Stripe with everything outsourced, targeting 1,000 subscribers at $20 profit each. The origin was personal: Mike's wife has an autoimmune disorder, they were following elimination diets and could not find grass-fed beef, so he was buying trash bags of meat from a farmer in a parking lot and selling steaks to friends. The model was set at $129 per box with a target of $20 fully loaded gross profit…

**Diagnosis.** Not a diagnosis of a broken business - this is the counter-example to CustomMade. The structural constraint Mike names is consumption, not acquisition: the biggest driver of churn is that customers leave meat in the freezer and stop cooking it, so they cancel. Secondary constraints: churn of about 3%/month means 12,000 new signups a month just to stand still; the fixed $169 box price cannot absorb meat inflation, so stacking ribeyes destroys gross margin while cheap cuts inflate it, putting the pricing model out of alignment with the customer; and top-of-funnel awareness on Meta became very…

**Intervention.**

- Pre-sell instead of raising: run a Kickstarter campaign rather than taking investment, so the market funds the inventory and validates demand.
- Reverse-engineer the Kickstarter verified badge - study which campaigns earned it, then generate day-one momentum (sold $40,000 on day one against a $25,000 target) to earn it, which pushed the campaign beyond their own audience to $210,000 in pre-sales.
- Add a stretch-goal bonus: free bacon in the first box if the campaign hits $100,000, which made buyers promote it.
- Stay capital-light on inventory: sell first, then decide what goes in the box, so no expensive ribeye inventory is held.
- Do the unscalable work: ship all 1,100 boxes within a week, then call every single buyer - 1,100 handwritten cards and personal phone calls - converting about 40% to subscribers.
- Outsource the work the founder will not do - hire the phone caller at $10/hour plus a $5 spiff rather than forcing himself to make 1,100 calls.
- Reverse-engineer another company's influencer list: concatenate Thrive Market's /partner/1, /partner/2 URLs to extract 400 health-and-wellness influencers with contact details, then cold outreach.
- Use a Trojan horse to open the conversation: offer to include the influencer's recipe in every box (they had no recipes and customers wanted them), which guaranteed a reply and turned into a business conversation.
- Pay influencers in commissions for life - $10-$15 per subscriber per month for as long as they stay - because there was no money upfront; dedicated email blasts with a last-chance offer converted, tweets and Facebook posts did not.
- Keep a bug that worked: when the free-bacon tech sent bacon to everyone and could not be turned off, make 'get free bacon' the offer - and later upgrade it to bacon for life, then stack ground beef for life and other for-life offers, sold even to existing customers for $50.
- Hire the expert at the right moment: pull the retired meat and seafood buyer out of retirement (found via LinkedIn) to buy meat and seafood, after setting the test 'if he saves me 25 cents a pound this pays for itself' - he delivered $1.50/pound.
- Own only the single point of failure: keep everything outsourced (the Toyota approach - work with partners, hold them to tight specs) except dry ice, because without dry ice no box ships.
- Keep partners rather than churning them: quarterly business reviews and audits where ButcherBox tells suppliers what they are doing wrong so they can fix it.
- Run a barbell hiring strategy - hire at both ends of the career (very young and retired) and avoid the middle - and write down core values so culture is hired for rather than assumed.
- Use profit to buy back shares annually (with a 409A valuation, and one year a reverse Dutch auction) so early employees get liquidity without an IPO or a sale.
- Acquire a media business (Truffle Shuffle, a live virtual cooking-class company) and use its content to solve the real churn driver - inspiring customers to cook the meat they already have - with Hormozi arguing the content should be pushed public rather than kept behind the member paywall, to…
- Referral programme: let members refer a friend for a trial box at $20 shipping and handling, giving the referrer nothing - because every incentive they tested performed worse than simply letting members give their friends meat.

**Result.** Revenue went from about $200,000 in the Kickstarter to roughly $500,000, then $5M, $33M, $105M, $220M, then $450M in the COVID year, with $450M, $550M and $570M in the following years, before the first down year in 2023 and a return to about 6% growth. Mike owns 70% and has bought back $20-30M of shares from early holders. The business has 430,000 customers, churns about 3%/month, retains about 60% of first-year customers, has an NPS of 63, has shipped to 1.7-1.75 million households, and runs…

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Kickstarter result | **$40,000 day one, $210,000 total pre-sales** |
| revenue trajectory | **$200K -> $500K -> $5M -> $33M -> $105M -> $220M -> $450M** |
| current revenue | **$550,000,000** |
| gross profit target per box | **$20 fully loaded** |
| gross margin | **about 30%, down to 25% after inflation and two price rises** |
| net margin | **about 6%** |
| customers | **430,000** |
| monthly churn | **about 3%** |
| signups needed to stand still | **12,000/month, about 400/day** |
| year-one retention | **about 60%** |
| households shipped to | **1.7-1.75 million** |
| Kickstarter to subscriber conversion by phone | **about 40%** |
| meat buyer's delivered saving | **$1.50/pound against a $0.25 target** |
| ownership | **70%** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Fund the business with the customer's money, not an investor's: pre-sell, then reverse-engineer whatever mechanic gives you free reach (here the Kickstarter verified badge), and add a stretch-goal bonus so buyers promote for you. Then do the unscalable work that actually creates the first cohort - ship fast, phone every buyer, handwrite the cards - and buy your way out of the work you personally will not do. Build your outreach list by reverse-engineering a bigger competitor's partner page. Pay affiliates in commissions for life rather than upfront, because you have no money and they want…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The video title says $600,000,000/yr; Mike corrects it on camera to '550'. The title figure is Hormozi's, not the operator's.
- The revenue series is spoken as a list without years ('200', '500 grand', '5 million', '33 million', '105 million 220'), so only the $450M COVID year and the 2023 decline are anchored to a period; the rest is a sequence, not a dated series.
- The 'free bacon' origin is a bug, not a designed offer - any summary presenting it as intentional product strategy loses the actual lesson (they could not turn it off, so they sold it).
- Net margin is stated two ways in quick succession ('they're like six' and 'six and a half last year') - both are recorded as stated.
- ButcherBox is described as profitable since day one and never having run out of money, yet also as having gone to a 25% gross margin and 6% net after two price increases - the transcript does not reconcile the day-one profitability claim with the later margin compression.
- The acquisition of Truffle Shuffle is discussed at length but the price is explicitly withheld ('I don't think I could talk about'), so no figure is recorded.

## How I built a 1.2M follower audience in 6 months
`WrCt0R3FBFs` · https://youtu.be/WrCt0R3FBFs

*The full content-creation model behind growing a 180k audience to 1.2M in six months: test on Twitter, record, add call-to-actions, contextualize per platform, then multiply volume — plus the language shift ('how I' not 'how to') and reciprocity math that make it work.*

### Case study

**Business.** His own audience/content business: Acquisition.com's media engine (YouTube, Instagram, Twitter/X, podcast) feeding a book and a high-ticket consulting offer for businesses doing $3M+

**Starting state.** 180,000-person audience across all channels, accumulated over 12 months. Posting 7 times a week: 3 YouTube videos, 3 podcasts, 1 Instagram post. Podcast at 20,000 downloads/month. No call-to-actions in the content. He had never framed himself as a content creator.

**Diagnosis.** Two constraints. (1) Volume: the input was a normal level of output, and the gap to outliers is orders of magnitude, not 2x-10x — Cardone was posting 5x more. (2) Authority: he was delivering theoretical/industry-level claims ('how to', 'you should') from a position he had not earned, instead of experience-level claims ('how I', 'what I did for client X'), which triggers the unspoken question 'why should I listen to you?' He had been putting the ladder against the wrong wall — trying to build something he did not have the authority to presume.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Test: move idea capture from emailing himself to public Twitter/X posts, which doubles as a fast, unlimited-volume testing ground.
- 2. Record: turn the highest-engagement tweets into shorts and threads into long videos.
- 3. Add call-to-actions: operationalize ~6 standard CTAs x 5 variants each = ~30 rotating CTAs, 5-10 seconds each, injected at the beginning, middle and end (plus extra mid-rolls on long content) to avoid banner/audio blindness.
- 4. Contextualize: make thumbnail, caption and text native to each destination platform instead of reposting the same TikTok with watermark and caption everywhere.
- 5. Distribute at volume: scale from 7 to 80 posts per week across all platforms.
- 6. Shift the language: speak only about what he has done — 'how I' not 'how to', 'what my clients did' not 'what you should do'.
- 7. Give away the secrets and sell the implementation, so much value that it feels uncomfortable, relying on reciprocity to drive the paid rung.
- 8. Make the free content better than competitors' paid content, because the price of free is still time and attention and it has to clear that bar.

**Result.** Audience went from 180,000 (12 months of work) to 1.2 million in the following 6 months. Podcast went from 20,000 to 400,000 downloads per month. He describes the outcome as a 10x increase in growth rate, matching the 10x input increase in content volume.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Audience before/after | **180,000 -> 1.2 million** |
| Time to build each audience level | **180,000 in 12 months; 1.2 million in 6 months** |
| Posting volume before/after | **7/week -> 80/week** |
| Podcast downloads before/after | **20,000/month -> 400,000/month** |
| Content volume vs growth rate equivalence | **10x in, 10x out** |

> **Transferable pattern.** The lever was not a better hook or a new platform — it was (a) multiplying output by ~10x, and (b) changing the grammatical subject of every claim from 'you' to 'I'. Volume removes the strategy-vs-execution confusion (you can't diagnose strategy at 300 flyers), and 'how I' removes the authority objection that kills unknown operators. Then convert the free attention with short, rotating, native-to-platform call-to-actions, and monetize only the implementation. If you are getting normal results, audit whether your output is normal and whether your claims are ones you've earned the right to make.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The written 'give away the secrets' summary usually omits the reciprocity LADDER mechanic: the next rung is only sellable if the previous rung delivered value in excess of its price. Once value is squeezed equal to price you get a satisfied customer, not a raving one, and the ascension stops.
- Framework summaries present content volume as a growth tactic; here he quantifies it as 7 -> 80 posts/week with a 10x growth-rate result and explicitly warns the required increase is often 100x-300x, not 10x.
- The 'why should I listen to you' authority test and the 'how I' vs 'how to' language pivot are usually stated as branding advice without the mechanism: you cannot be challenged on your own experience, only on your theory.
- Framework summaries of closing rarely include the concentric-circles ordering (circumstances -> other people -> avoidance), which determines how many overcomes remain before you reach someone who is actually in charge of the decision.
- His published frameworks do not include the 30-rotating-CTA / 5-10-second CTA operational detail, which is what he credits for the podcast going 20k -> 400k downloads/month.

## Building a $1,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 69 Minutes
`Wr6n_zNKvMk` · https://youtu.be/Wr6n_zNKvMk

*A live teardown of a $642k-revenue trash-collection business losing $151k: he forces a single avatar (scatter, not HOAs), a single channel (door-to-door), and rebuilds the offer into an A/B anchor whose blended upfront cash per door ($270) clears the fully-loaded breakeven ($208).*

### Case study

**Business.** Garby Disposal Services — residential trash, recycling and yard waste collection in Centreville/Chantilly/Clifton/Fairfax, Virginia. Owner: Philip. Two customer avatars (scatter/residential and HOAs) and four-plus acquisition channels (door-to-door, Meta ads, cold email, handwritten letters, referrals).

**Starting state.** Revenue $642,000, net profit -$151,000, net margin -23%, gross margin 8% (dragged down by ~$100,000 of one-off repairs on a single truck). 2,500 customers in just under 2 years. Scatter: 1,000 customers, $29.67/month billed quarterly at $89 with 3 months free, CAC $51, LTV $1,000 (21:1), 26-40% gross margin. HOA: 13 customers, ~$300,000 revenue, CAC $1,200, LTV $23,000 (18:1), 23% gross margin. Blended CAC $67, blended LTV $1,300, monthly churn 0.4%. Door-to-door: 300 doors/week at ~26% close,…

**Diagnosis.** Spread thin: two avatars and five channels, so nothing is being done well. But the binding constraint is not leads or margin — it is UPFRONT CASH. Because customers pay quarterly while fulfillment costs (labor, dump fees) accrue monthly, the business has to fund months 2 and 3 out of pocket, plus the $116 bin, plus the $50 commission. He solves for the exact number: $158 true setup cost + $50 commission = $208 of cash needed per door, versus the $89 (plus a bin they were giving away) they were collecting. Secondary diagnosis: HOAs are a commoditized lowest-bid auction that will squeeze them…

**Intervention.**

- 1. Pick one avatar: SCATTER (residential), not HOA. Rationale: HOAs are a race to the bottom on bids; scatter allows aggressive pricing, higher gross margin, out-marketing the competition, and once-weekly collection which raises throughput per truck. Inbound HOAs may still be closed but are not the…
- 2. Pick one channel: door-to-door. Kill Meta ads and cold outreach entirely — all attention to recruiting commission-only door knockers.
- 3. Rebuild the offer as an A/B anchor to clear $208 blended cash per door. Offer A (core): 3 months at $30 = $90, plus a $99 bin fee the customer owns (take the bin back if they cancel early) = $189 all-in, then ~$60/month. Offer B (anchor): prepay 12 months at $30/month = $360 and the $99 bin is…
- 4. Rename the fees to what the customer values: the 'bin fee' is really covering the $42 first-quarter labor, and the 'initiation fee' is really the commission. Waive the $49 setup fee entirely.
- 5. Add a QR-code lever: put a huge ugly QR code on every bin; customers pay $5/month extra to have it removed. Free advertising either way.
- 6. Add a 3% processing fee, waived if the customer puts a second payment method on file (which also removes failed-payment friction).
- 7. For prospects who refuse to buy the bin: finance it over 3 years at $150, which creates a 3-year term and lets you add a 4% annual price increase.
- 8. Recruit two to ten commission-only reps via Indeed/Craigslist ads written to the salesperson (headline, promise of six figures, 4-or-8-hour choice, damaging admission), then a 2-minute group call, then in-person, then job offers on the spot. Expect to hire five to get one. Screen for…
- 9. Sales training: a four-question script, 2-minute sale. Drill the door-open and first five seconds until it is nailed every time; role-play between doors; then document, demonstrate, duplicate (owner rides shotgun and gives immediate feedback).
- 10. The owner should never knock alone — always take a trainee so selling and training happen in the same hours. Offer the eventual lead trainer $60/sale instead of $50.
- 11. Buy a second truck when volume requires it; capacity is ~3,500 customers.

**Result.** Not reported in this video — the session ends with the plan and a prioritized recap. Hormozi's projections inside the conversation: with 10 reps at 5 sales/day that is 50 sales/day and 1,500 sales/month (which he says overshoots the goal by ~8x); with just the owner plus one rep doing 10 deals/day they would be at 300/month, hitting the extra 1,000 customers within about 3 months. Outcome stated as: cash flow positive.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting revenue | **$642,000** |
| Starting loss | **-$151,000 / -23% net margin** |
| Breakeven cash needed per door | **$208** |
| New blended cash per door after the anchor offer | **$270 (vs $190 core offer, vs $208 needed)** |
| Anchor take rate assumption | **20% take the 12-month anchor, 80% take the core** |
| Projected scale with 10 reps | **50 sales/day, 1,500/month** |
| Time to close the 1,000-customer gap | **~3 months at 10 deals/day between the owner and one rep** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When a business is unprofitable but the unit economics are actually fine (18:1 and 21:1 LTV:CAC), the constraint is almost never leads or margin — it is the timing of cash. Compute the exact fully-loaded cost of acquiring and setting up one customer (COGS-to-first-payment + CAC + commission), then redesign the OFFER so that average upfront cash collected exceeds that number, using an anchor option at the top rather than raising the core price. Anchors work on blended averages: if even 20% take the higher-commitment option, the average per-unit cash rises enough to fund growth debt-free, and…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Framework summaries treat 'pick one avatar and one channel' as generic focus advice; here it is quantified against a specific stage gate — one avatar, one channel, one product UP TO $1M or more.
- The offer literature rarely states the anchor mechanic as a blended-average cash play: you don't raise the core price, you add a top option and let a 20% take rate lift the average per-unit cash above the breakeven line.
- His published frameworks do not include the specific device of RENAMING fees to what the customer values (bin fee = the labor, initiation fee = the commission), which is what makes the added fees sellable.
- The 'sell the bin' tactic — charging for an asset you were previously giving away, keeping it as collateral, and financing it over 3 years with an annual escalator for refusers — is absent from the generic offer material.
- The recruiting material elsewhere in his corpus does not contain the 'hire five to get one', group-call-not-1:1, screen-for-crazies, offer-on-the-spot sequence for commission-only field sales.
- The compounding effect of always selling with a trainee present ('double dipping on effort') is not in the standard sales-team frameworks.

## Building a $2,300,000/yr Business for a Stranger in 57 Mins
`-Koq14DPXC4` · https://youtu.be/-Koq14DPXC4

*A live teardown of a 7-location, $2.36M eyelash salon chain at 28% net margin: resolve the dead-weight partnership first, then add weekend surge pricing, convert rebooking into a sales process (BAM FAM), rebuild the membership as an opt-out default, install a 6-step pay-and-skill ladder, and fix ad attribution — worth a 2-3x on the business.*

### Case study

**Business.** Amy Lash and Beauty — eyelash extension salons (also facials, product sales). Owner: Annie/Anie. Seven locations, 10+ years, 20,000+ clients served. Two layers of management (a manager per location). Three sets of partners, including two full-time partners and one long-standing partner she co-owns multiple locations with.

**Starting state.** Revenue $2,364,000 at 28% net margin (~$600,000 profit before splitting with partners, and she takes no salary for the marketing and scaling work she does). Service pricing $170-$300 for a set, $99 intro promo, $70-$270 refills. Lash artists paid 50% of topline with all costs (lashes, rent, marketing) on the business — meaning everything else runs on 22%. 1,700 appointments and 1,100 guests per month, 30% new / 70% returning, 50% of clients stay past 3 months. Google ads $1,000/month (~0.5% of…

**Diagnosis.** Three layers, in priority order. (1) THE PARTNERSHIP IS THE CONSTRAINT — it consumes ~80% of her mental bandwidth, and none of the operational fixes will be executed while it is unresolved. Underneath it: she gave away ownership where she should have given a profit share, and she has never been paid market rate for the manager role she performs, which makes the business look more profitable than it is and makes scaling impossible. (2) THE MONEY IS IN THE UNSELLED UPSELLS — the $99 promo is a lead magnet that breaks even; the business is the upsell. She personally upsells at 90% while the team…

**Intervention.**

- 1. Resolve the partnership FIRST, before any operational work. Three ranked paths: (A) pay her market rate as manager via an increased profit share; (B) a shotgun offer — buy me out at this price, or I'll buy you out at the same price; (C) an equity swap — consolidate locations so each partner owns…
- 2. Convert the other partner's 33% ownership into a monthly profit-share bonus (not equity), and give the partner who is 'half out the door' a 12-18 month buyout in exchange for helping replace her.
- 3. Weekend surge pricing: +10% (down from his proposed +20%) on Thursday/Friday/Saturday, framed as the standard price with the rest of the week discounted. Grandfather existing regulars into old pricing as a membership benefit — create the problem, then sell the solution.
- 4. Make rebooking mandatory via BAM FAM: book the next appointment at the front desk — and do it BEFORE the service, because once they have received the value they want to leave. Train two scripted overcomes ('I'm not sure' / 'I don't have my card') and use the card on file.
- 5. Rebuild the membership as an opt-out default: 'you've already been paying for this and opted in — we just need to formalize it.' Keep the price the same and add value instead of discounting: free facials each visit, product discounts, referral bonus raised from $10 to $50, anniversary and…
- 6. Sequence the membership sale as a three-step ladder: (i) BAM FAM the next appointment (easy win), (ii) offer the free thing, (iii) convert to membership. Only after membership is agreed, ask 'would you like to save some money?' and step up to prepay 6 or 12 months — at checkout, framed as 'do…
- 7. Install a 6-step career ladder: six title changes and six pay changes every 3 months (junior/normal/senior technician, then junior/senior artist), starting at 40% and rising to 50-55%. Each title change also unlocks a new sellable skill so the artist earns more and the business charges more.…
- 8. Fix the front-end guest process (before the service): collect ID, confirm/collect the card on file, have them sign in with a dropdown for 'where did you hear about us' plus a referral code, and get reviews — all while they wait. This produces the attribution data needed to scale ad spend.
- 9. Hire one person at $40,000/year whose only job is to call leads within 1 minute. He ranks this as priority #1 of the recap.
- 10. Train via 30 minutes of daily role play between staff, drilling the exact scripts with immediate correction and repetition — 'don't just say here, say these words.'

**Result.** Not reported in this video — it ends with the prioritized plan. His modelled impacts: 10% weekend surcharge = ~5% revenue = 28% to 33% net margin = ~20% profit increase; lifting 3-month retention from 50% to 70%+ = 20-30% lift in the business; prepayment at checkout = ~20% lift; lead follow-up hire = 2-3x the business. Combined, he frames the plan as worth 2-3x.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting revenue and margin | **$2,364,000 at 28% net margin** |
| Profit pool before partner split | **~$600,000** |
| Marketing spend as % of revenue | **0.5% ($12,000 on $2.3M); 1% would be $23,000** |
| Weekend surcharge agreed | **+10% on Thu/Fri/Sat** |
| Retention target and its modelled lift | **50% -> 70%+ = 20-30% lift** |
| Lead follow-up hire | **$40,000/year, 2-3x the business** |
| Upsell conversion with default framing | **20-40% -> 80-90%** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Before fixing the machine, remove the handbrake. When an owner is burning most of their bandwidth on a partnership or a role conflict, every operational improvement you install will go unexecuted — so price the partnership first, even at a cost (give up the better location), because being unconstrained compounds. Two reusable mechanics carry the rest: (1) TURN EVERY REQUIRED RETURN VISIT INTO A SALES CONVERSATION — rebooking walks and talks like an admin task but it is a sale, and booking it BEFORE the service converts better because the customer has not yet received the value; (2) FRAME…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Framework summaries say 'give profit share not equity' without the reasoning: equity bundles risk, control, profit AND sale proceeds, and only the profit component is revocable — which is the whole point when rewarding a location manager.
- The rebooking play (BAM FAM) is usually presented as a scheduling tip; here it is explicitly a SALES conversation with scripted overcomes, a mandated pre-service timing rule, and a 2x-visits-per-year payoff quantified.
- Published offer material does not include the surge-pricing framing device: raise peak prices but present them as standard and off-peak as a discount, then sell 'no surge pricing' as the flagship membership benefit — create the problem, then sell the solution.
- The career-ladder detail (six title changes + six pay changes every 3 months, with each title unlocking a new sellable skill, on a 40% to 55% commission scale) is more specific than any general 'career path' advice in his corpus.
- The 'free instead of discount' rule is usually stated qualitatively; here he adds the constraint that each individual bonus should be worth as much as the entire price on its own, and points to a specific book page (117) for the bonus-stacking method.
- Framework summaries omit the owner-salary adjustment entirely — that artificially high margins from unpaid owner labour will break the model at scale, and that this must be factored into return-on-capital before deciding to open more locations.

## Building a $3,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 51 Mins
`BMF2fWHyDrg` · https://youtu.be/BMF2fWHyDrg

*A teardown of a 40-year-old, $1.72M custom trophy business running at 6.4% net margin: shut the money-losing retail location (+50% profit instantly), switch from cost-plus to value-based pricing with rolling price tests (a 6% raise doubles profit), max out the 13:1 SEO channel, go all-in on TikTok organic, and start emailing the 10,000-person list that is doing nothing.*

### Case study

**Business.** Trophy Outlet (trophyoutlet.com) — custom trophies, awards and personalization, plus a separate gag-gift brand (funny signs, 'head mofo in charge' style gifts) sold on Amazon, Etsy and TikTok Shop. Third-generation family business, started 1985 (40th year), one retail location plus one production facility, ~$1.72M revenue. Owner: Cody Schulson.

**Starting state.** Revenue $1.72M, profit ~$110,000, net margin 6.4%, gross margin 40%. LTV $133, CAC ~$11.90, 11:1 blended LTV:CAC (gross profit based). Website: 990,000 visits, 2,500 orders, 2.8% conversion, 781 SKUs, all made to order. Channels: SEO/agency, Meta (started Oct/Nov), Amazon ($7,100/month agency + ads), Etsy, TikTok Shop ($2,000 so far). Channel returns: direct/internal 13:1, Amazon 99.6% conversion, TikTok AOV ~$20. Revenue split ~50/50 new vs returning, with $530,000/year coming through internal…

**Diagnosis.** Not a volume problem and not a fixed-cost problem — a PRICING problem plus an attention problem. His test: the business gets $530,000/year in free, word-of-mouth return customers and STILL only nets 6.4%, so either fixed costs are high (they aren't) or the products are mispriced. Confirmed: there is no pricing discipline at all, and cost-plus pricing means margin is whatever is left over. Second diagnosis: he is running TWO businesses (B2B/bread-and-butter trophies and D2C gag gifts) and pursuing both means serving neither; he has to pick. Third: he is spreading attention across four-plus…

**Intervention.**

- 1. CONSOLIDATE: shut the losing retail location. Costs ~no revenue (little foot traffic), adds ~$50,000/year straight to the bottom line = +50% profit, and consolidates his attention; bring the best people to home base and 'release to free agency' the rest.
- 2. PRICING: switch from cost-plus to value-based pricing. Two paths — (a) rolling ~5-6% monthly price increases and keep going, or (b) 80/20 split tests on the highest-sales-velocity items. Start the tests on the gag gifts (not price sensitive) and then on the 'boring' trophies. Optimize gross…
- 3. SEO: go back to the agency and ask them to 'max me out' — 3x the backlinks and 3x the articles. It is outsourced, so it costs him no time, and it returns 13:1.
- 4. PPC: buy his own brand terms and derivatives (and long-tail associated terms) via Google Ads — one-time setup, cheap, near-guaranteed return.
- 5. TikTok VOLUME: go from 1 to 3 posts/day and treat the cap as nonexistent. Focus on trends and memes — hire a 17-year-old to scroll and tell you what is trending. Repurpose to Instagram for free extra reach.
- 6. INFLUENCERS/AFFILIATES: push TikTok Shop affiliates hard (his TikTok rep already told him this). Product price point ($20-50) is ideal for creator content.
- 7. TIKTOK ADS: build the loop — organic content (10% wins) -> put ad spend behind winners -> send winners to influencers as the creative brief -> their versions feed your next content. Stay hook-centric and reuse winning hooks.
- 8. IN-BOX OFFER: because he fulfils his own orders, insert a card in every box with a QR code, the top 3 gag gifts, and a buy-one-get-two-free offer, with the single-unit price fixed so the math works.
- 9. EMAIL: build two programs — behavioural flows (5-email sequences for product views, two-step opt-ins, abandoned carts, with a 'reply back with the funniest trophy' hook to boost deliverability) and long-term nurture at 1x/week (52 emails/year, all text, link to images). Content angle:…
- 10. STRATEGY: pick ONE path. He framed it as D2C/media (arbitrage media and sell gag gifts at scale, exit potential lower) vs B2B/leagues (outbound sales team, 'your trophy provider for life', slower to build but more valuable and more sellable). Cody chose the TikTok/D2C route for scalability.

**Result.** Not reported in this video — it ends with a 9-item prioritized plan and the owner's reaction ('much cleaner and simpler than I thought'). Modelled impacts stated during the session: price test = 2x profit on its own (potentially 4-5x if he can push 25%); closing the location = +50% profit; SEO max-out = ~50% revenue boost; PPC = 10-20% boost; email = ~$1.5M sitting unused; TikTok mastery = the lever from $1M to $10M.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting revenue and net margin | **$1.72M at 6.4% net margin ($110,000 profit)** |
| Profit effect of shutting the losing location | **+50% profit, ~$50,000/year** |
| Profit effect of a 6% price increase | **~2x profit** |
| Unused email opportunity | **~$1.5M on a 10,000-contact list** |
| SEO channel return and headroom | **13:1 LTV:CAC; 50% of revenue; ~50% boost available** |
| Viral proof point for TikTok | **$250,000 in one month from a viral video** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When a business is profitable but barely, check the PRICE before the funnel. The diagnostic test: if the highest-quality, zero-acquisition-cost segment (word-of-mouth return customers) is still not making you rich, and your fixed costs are not high, you are mispriced — full stop. Pricing is the highest-return, lowest-drag lever available (you change a number, not a process), and at single-digit net margins a 6% price increase is roughly a 100% profit increase. So: run rolling small price tests on your highest-velocity SKUs, optimize gross profit x units sold rather than conversion rate, and…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Framework summaries present value-based pricing as a principle; here he gives the operational version — rolling 5-6% monthly increases, or 80/20 split tests on the highest-velocity items, optimizing gross profit x units sold rather than conversion rate.
- The quantified profit leverage of pricing at thin margins (a 6% increase roughly doubling profit at a 6.4% net margin, and 25% potentially being 4-5x profit) is the crux of this teardown and is not usually stated with numbers.
- The 'return customers are free sales, so they should be your most profitable segment' test is a concrete diagnostic for detecting mispricing that does not appear in the general framework material.
- His email guidance here is unusually specific and usually absent: two separate programs (behavioural flows vs long-term nurture), all-text emails with links to images for deliverability, a reply-to-enter hook on the first email, and a cadence that starts at 1x/week for infrequent-purchase…
- The in-box insert offer (BOGO with the single-unit price fixed so the math works) is a physical-product tactic that the general offer frameworks do not cover.
- The content -> ads -> influencers -> content loop (organic winners brief the influencers, influencer output briefs your next organic) is a specific operating loop rather than generic 'post more' advice.

## Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke
`oys_fv25SYM` · https://youtu.be/oys_fv25SYM

*His own escape-from-poverty playbook, in order: say 'it's my fault', use what you have (even if what you have is anger), spend less than you make, pour every excess dollar into skills, and shed the friends who decrease the odds you hit your goal.*

### Case study

**Business.** Autobiographical — his own escape from poverty and the business trajectory that followed (personal training -> gyms -> licensing -> acquisition.com). Not a stranger's teardown; the 'case' is his own.

**Starting state.** Broke, working a white-collar consulting job he had taken a step down from to earn minimum wage in a gym. First brick-and-mortar storefront at 23, doing the cleaning, billing, sales, teaching and equipment repair himself because he didn't know you could hire employees and couldn't afford to. Moved across the country from Baltimore to Huntington Beach knowing nobody. Working seven days a week, every waking hour. Wrote down a goal of $10,000/month income 13 years before this video. Had reached…

**Diagnosis.** Two root causes. (1) He was in the powerless/victim frame — blaming his parents, his circumstances, other people — and 'whatever you cast blame to is where you also cast power to'. (2) He had no plan B other than the thing he refused to go back to, which is what produced the willingness to eat the glass. Note the nuance: the fix was not positivity. Affirmations and 'follow your passion' did not work for him because nothing made him feel happy — the fuel was anger and the refusal to let the people back home be right.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Say 'it's my fault' — own everything up to this moment (missed Mondays, skipped diets, unsaved money). This is the concrete foundation everything else is poured on.
- 2. Use what you have, not what you wish you had. The fuel available was anger, shame and pain; he used them rather than waiting to feel passionate or positive.
- 3. Live one person's normal life PLUS the workday. Your job covers today; the extra hours are what buy tomorrow.
- 4. Spend less than you make; take all the excess and spend it on making more — reinvest stored energy into potential energy. His trade: spend $2,000 to go from $5,000/month to $6,000/month.
- 5. Buy skills, not things. Measure in skills, not money. Take every dollar you can and buy more skills; later, buy other people's years of skills by hiring them.
- 6. Learn to sell by selling something — enrol in affiliate/ambassador programs so you only have to figure out one skill at a time; then take on more responsibility for a bigger share of the nut.
- 7. Build authority by accumulating evidence: learn it, get good, get proof, and let people ask you for help — then build the business around what they ask about.
- 8. Reframe failed experiments as experience points rather than a return to zero.
- 9. Audit and shed friends who decrease the probability of hitting the goal — and accept the social consequences, because if you didn't want to go it is a win-win.
- 10. Future-pace the alternative: deliberately imagine the specific pain of not changing until the pain of staying the same exceeds the pain of changing.
- 11. Take the next step regardless of emotional state — anger, sadness, shame all work; only the step matters.

**Result.** First $100,000 took 5 years, saved $1 at a time. Six gyms by age 26, all cash-flowed. Licensing business at $4 million/month. Later, the people asking him for help escalated with each tier (personal training clients -> gym owners -> licensing operators -> large-business owners), which is the ladder that produced his consulting and content business.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Time to first $100,000 | **5 years** |
| Gyms owned by 26 | **6 gyms, all cash-flowed** |
| Licensing business revenue | **$4 million/month** |
| First paid consultation | **$200** |
| The reinvestment trade | **$2,000 spent to raise monthly income from $5,000 to $6,000** |

> **Transferable pattern.** The order matters and the first step is psychological, not tactical: you cannot change a situation you are still blaming on something else, because blame is where you hand over your power. So the sequence is (1) own it entirely, (2) use whatever fuel you actually have — anger and shame work as well as passion — (3) take only the next step, never plan the whole path, (4) spend less than you make and put every excess dollar into skills rather than into feeling better or looking better, and (5) treat failed experiments as experience points rather than losses. Two reusable heuristics carry the…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- This is the least tactical and most autobiographical Tier A video in the batch: there is no teardown of a stranger's business, so the case_study is his own trajectory. Downstream consumers should not treat its numbers as client results.
- The general 'follow your passion / positive mindset' framing is explicitly contradicted here: he says affirmations and positivity did not work for him, and that anger was the fuel that got him started — 'nothing made me feel happy'.
- The psychological precondition ('it's my fault' / 'I am source') is usually omitted from the tactical frameworks even though he says 90% of people never clear it.
- The friend-audit heuristic (increase or decrease the probability of failure, no in-between) plus the 'no social obligations, only social consequences' rule is a decision procedure absent from his written frameworks.
- The 'buy skills, not things' rule is stated with a concrete mechanism: in the beginning you buy all your own skills, then later you buy other people's 10 years of skills by hiring them ('buying other people's lives').
- The failed-experiment-as-experience-point reframe (you are not back at zero) is a specific way of accounting for losses that the general material does not state.

## Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 31 Minutes | Scale or Fail
`j2TZMFkj71Q` · https://youtu.be/j2TZMFkj71Q

*A Scale-or-Fail teardown of an AU$1.1M sticker-teaching business with a 22% bootcamp-to-membership conversion: the constraints are ad volume (she makes 4 creatives, she needs 80-200), ad spend cadence (front-load the last 3 days), awareness-level hooks, and an annual-only offer with a physical bundle as the premium — plus a wilder test of making the bootcamp a 7-day trial of the membership.*

### Case study

**Business.** Mim Jenkinson's sticker-teaching business — she teaches crafters how to make stickers. Low-ticket digital products with a main membership (Secret Sticker Society, $27/month or $217/year) and many interchangeable low-ticket upsells. Acquisition runs through a live paid bootcamp launched three times a year. 20,000+ crafters taught over 10 years. Two employees (one is her husband).

**Starting state.** AU$1.1M revenue (~US$800k) in the last 12 months — her first seven-figure year after 10 years, with multiple seven figures cumulative. Profit margin 30-35% (~$500k). Bootcamp ticket $10 (paid, no free option). 22% of ticket buyers convert into the membership. Front-end AOV ~$36 against a $37 cost to acquire — roughly break-even on the front end, always profitable by the end of the event. Ad spend on the last launch: only $16,000, with a self-imposed CPA cap that has never exceeded ~$50.…

**Diagnosis.** A PURE DEMAND problem, not a delivery problem — doubling customers breaks nothing. The real constraints are three self-imposed ones plus one structural one: (1) she caps ad spend for no good reason when she is highly profitable and her CPA has never exceeded $50 against a $100+ willingness to pay; (2) she is spending too late and too evenly instead of front-loading the last three days of the launch; (3) she is starved of creative — 4 ads instead of the hundreds the account needs, and no system to generate them; (4) her ads are bottom-funnel (product/offer aware) so performance collapses as…

**Intervention.**

- 1. OFFER: make the annual the ONLY offer available at the next launch — do not mention the monthly at all. After the cart closes, run everyone else to the monthly without bonuses.
- 2. Add a physical bundle (the sticker kit they need to do the thing anyway) as the annual-only premium, priced as a $149 decoy so the annual is the obvious choice. He expects this to move annual take from 30% to ~50%.
- 3. Replace/augment the checkout bump (currently a $47 course at 30%) with the physical bundle at ~$99.
- 4. Raise the effective price point of the event: a full five-day event can support a $300 ticket; accept conversion halving if AOV goes to $300, because it gives her $150+ in the first 30 days, which is the confidence threshold to spend more.
- 5. SPEND CADENCE: 5-10% of spend in week one purely to test creative; flat in the middle; 60-70% in the peak week with up to 50% of total spend in the final three days.
- 6. SPEND VOLUME: remove the self-imposed cap and be willing to pay a $100 CPA. She accepts the challenge.
- 7. CREATIVE VOLUME: take her 20 highest-converting ads of all time and re-shoot each in four different settings/outfits/backgrounds = 80 ads. Clip every live Q&A into organic and paid creative. Use member screenshots, sticker images and AI statics. Run an activation ('make a sticker in your first 7…
- 8. HOOKS / AWARENESS: move up-funnel to pain/problem-aware hooks rather than product/offer-aware ones, so performance holds as spend scales. Go sub-specific with call-outs — '100 ponds and no oceans'.
- 9. THE WILD TEST (V2): position the bootcamp itself as a 7-day trial of the $27 membership (optionally a $1 trial with card on file). Front-end conversion goes to 100% because everyone is in the membership by default and must cancel; then push everyone to the annual. Model: 55% of the 100 trialists…
- 10. TRACKING: optimize campaigns around purchases and start reporting EPCs (earnings per click) so she knows what a click is worth and can price her bids confidently.
- 11. Keep making more organic content to feed the list.

**Result.** Verdict delivered in-video: 'you will be scaling with me.' No revenue result yet — she reports early-stage promotion for the next launch moving in the right direction, and confirms the previous piece of advice (pitching annual) doubled her average cart value. Hormozi's stated view: very few universes where adding the physical premium and presenting annual-only does not generate more revenue up front, and the plan has the potential to 5x or 10x the business.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting revenue and margin | **AU$1.1M (~US$800k) at 30-35% profit** |
| Front-end conversion and AOV | **22% convert to membership; AOV ~$36 vs ~$37 to acquire** |
| Annual take rate after pitching annual | **10% -> 30%** |
| The trial-test model | **55 retained x $300 LTV = ~$16,500 vs ~$10-11,000 = 50-60%…** |
| Target annual take rate with the premium | **~50%** |
| Creative target | **80 ads (20 winners x 4 settings), scaling to 200+ and…** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When the product and retention already work (22% conversion, 5% churn, 30-35% margins) and delivery does not break when you double volume, the constraint is never the product — it is that the owner has capped their own inputs. Three inputs to un-cap in order: (1) SPEND — if you are highly profitable and your CPA has never once exceeded $50, a self-imposed cap is pure fear, not strategy; set a CPA ceiling you are willing to pay and then actually pay it. (2) CREATIVE VOLUME — the account needs hundreds of ads, not four. Generate them from assets you already own: re-shoot your 20 all-time…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The 'physical product premium instead of a discount' tactic is more specific than the generic bonus-stacking advice: attach a physical bundle the customer must buy anyway, price it as a high decoy, and give it free only with the annual commitment.
- The ad spend cadence here is quantified in a way the general ad material is not: 5-10% week 1 for creative testing only, 60-70% in the peak week, and up to 50% of total spend in the final three days.
- The creative-volume math (20 all-time winners x 4 settings = 80; 200 customers = 200 ads via an activation) is a concrete system for generating ad volume rather than an exhortation to 'make more creative'.
- The awareness-level material is usually taught descriptively; here it is used diagnostically — bottom-funnel (offer-aware) ads are the specific reason performance collapses when you scale spend.
- The trial-as-front-end-offer move (make the paid event itself a trial of the continuity product so front-end conversion goes from 22% to 100%) is a structural inversion absent from the standard funnel frameworks.
- The cash-timing framing — get $150+ collected in the first 30 days so you can comfortably spend more — is stated here as the actual purpose of offer restructuring, not just profit.

## If You Have Less Than $10,000 Saved. Please Watch This Video...
`ymFWgFiKUvM` · https://youtu.be/ymFWgFiKUvM

*Six sequential money steps for someone broke: buy nothing, build a $1k work fund, kill consumer debt fastest-first for the psychological win, grow 3-6 months of expenses in cash, eliminate risky spending (cars first), then invest 15% pre-tax and another 15% into your own earning capacity.*

### Case study

**Business.** Autobiographical — his own personal-finance history and the businesses it funded (first gym at 23 -> gym turnarounds -> Gym Launch -> Prestige Labs -> Acquisition.com). Not a stranger's teardown.

**Starting state.** A white-collar consultant with $50,000 saved and a condo, earning $55,000-$60,000 in his first year out of college and $70,000-$80,000 the next. He wanted to start a gym but had no capital beyond those savings. Later, at $2,000/month income, he lived in a house with six roommates and shared a bedroom.

**Diagnosis.** The constraint on taking business risk was personal fixed costs, not business skill. If he had been forced into debt just to live, he would never have been able to take a second or third shot after the first business failed. So he treated personal risk as the thing to jam down to zero in order to go on the offensive on the business side.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Buy nothing. No discretionary spending at all while accumulating.
- 2. Save aggressively while employed: he saved $50,000 after tax out of a $55-80k salary.
- 3. Cut housing: sold the condo, drove across the country, rented a bedroom for $400/month, then lived inside his own gym at zero personal housing cost.
- 4. Keep the habit even after income rose — rent stayed at $1,200/month even at $1M/month income, and personal spend stayed under $15,000/month.
- 5. Protect the ability to take shots: because personal burn was near zero, he could fail 9 businesses and 7 partnerships and keep going.
- 6. Once there was surplus, reinvest into skills and businesses in a chain: gym -> gym turnaround -> Gym Launch -> Prestige Labs -> Acquisition.com.

**Result.** The chain of businesses he names came directly out of the low-burn position: gym -> gym turnaround -> Gym Launch -> Prestige Labs -> Acquisition.com. He reports living on less than $15,000/month while earning $1,000,000/month, and stopped checking his accounts daily once the business crossed ~$20 million.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Savings that funded the first gym | **$50,000 after tax on a $55-80k salary** |
| Personal burn at $1M/month income | **under $15,000/month; rent $1,200/month** |
| Failure count | **9 failed businesses, 7 failed partnerships** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Savings are not the goal — optionality is. The reason to keep personal fixed costs brutally low is not frugality for its own sake, it is that low personal risk lets you take more shots, and taking more shots is what eventually produces the win. He says this explicitly: if he had gone into debt just to live, he could not have taken the second and third shots after the first business failed. The operating rules are: (1) spend less than you make, permanently, at every income level — his rent stayed at $1,200/month at $1M/month income; (2) translate every recurring cost into working days so you…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The framework material says 'spend less than you make' as a principle; here it is quantified across income levels — rent still $1,200/month at $1M/month income, personal spend under $15,000/month.
- The reason for frugality is stated here as OPTIONALITY, not virtue: low personal burn increases your number of shots on goal and is what allowed 9 failed businesses and 7 failed partnerships without ending the game.
- The debt payoff guidance explicitly recommends the PSYCHOLOGICAL order (fastest first) over the mathematically optimal order (highest rate first) — a deliberate departure from standard financial advice.
- The money-to-time translation is given as a concrete measuring stick (a $600/month lease is 6 of 22 working days; with $1,200 rent, 18 of 22 days are gone), which is a more visceral tool than the usual 'latte factor' framing.
- The 15% + 15% split (15% pre-tax to investments, another 15% pre-tax to your own education/skills) is a specific allocation rule, with the explicit claim that investing in yourself beats the S&P 500 early on.
- The 30x12 challenge (30 days straight, 12 hours/day) is framed as a finite proof-of-capacity rather than a permanent schedule, which is not how hard-work advice is usually framed.

`MH-IMJxbUY4` · https://youtu.be/MH-IMJxbUY4

### Case study

**Business.** Just Get Out of Town (JGOOT) — a coaching and course business that teaches people to use credit cards to get vacations ('travel hedging'). Owner: Joel McDonald, age 53. Largest audience: retirees, empty nesters and business owners. Products: a book (front end, loss leader), mini-memberships, a $99 offer, a Facebook group, and a high-ticket coaching program. 12,000 clients served.

**Starting state.** $6.4M trailing 12-month revenue, ~30% profit margin, ROAS 4.5:1, LTV:CAC of only 1.4:1. 85% of customers come from the book funnel on Meta; 10% from conferences/meetups/guest podcasting; 5% from affiliates and charity partnerships. Hitting a ceiling at ~$100,000/month on Meta. He spent $150,000 in one month and got only 10% more book sales. The book is a loss leader with a ~6-month payback even including the back end. Outbound sales only started a month earlier; split is 60% inbound / 40%…

**Diagnosis.** The business is demand-constrained, and the constraint is NOT the channel or the offer — it is CREATIVE. Evidence: spending $150k in a month produced only 10% more book sales, which means Meta has exhausted the people the current creative can convert; the offer already converts, so don't touch it. Three consequences flow from that: (1) CAC stays high and LTV:CAC stays at a skinny 1.4:1; (2) the funnel's downstream conversion is being wasted because leads are not scored on the two factors that actually predict a sale; (3) he is leaving a bigger, colder market untouched — 'I started the company…

**Intervention.**

- 2. MODEL THE TOP TRAVEL PAGES: study the most viral content on the biggest travel Instagram pages and replicate the format, layering the offer over it ('seven hidden gems you've never heard of, for under $1,000'). Hire a native Gen Z creator who is plugged into the platforms and trending audio; do…
- 3. KALEIDOSCOPE the single highest-converting creative into 20-30 variants: black and white, sepia, 3-second AI video made from the still, cartoon, Ghibli, remakes/re-films. Do NOT change winning copy — he ran one copy version for 6 months and another for 3, and a company he owns spending a couple…
- 4. AI AVATARS: use AI-generated TikTok-style videos (15-30 seconds) with the hook, the three objections handled, and a CTA to the book funnel. Also put diverse avatars in the creative so the algorithm can expand into new lookalike audiences, since likeness is one of the strongest predictors of…
- 5. TEST ORGANIC FIRST, THEN CONVERT: post short-form organically, and when one wins, add a 5-second CTA to the end and run that exact post as an ad. A double dip — the content is free, and the winner becomes paid creative.
- 6. LEAD SCORING: the two factors that qualify the avatar are credit card spend (~$5,000/month) and vacation spend (~$5,000/year). Put both into the opt-in and score every lead — two-for-twos called first, one-of-twos second, zeros last.
- 7. OUTBOUND TEAM: with ~300 prospects/day entering the funnel, he needs ~6 reps on power dialers with a $300/day KPI each. Use a parallel dialer that calls 10 numbers at once at a ~5% pick-up rate, routing live connections to reps so talk time is maximised.

Before you open a second channel, exhaust the first: build a UGC loop so your customers generate your creative for you (gate something they want behind posting), kaleidoscope your single all-time winner into 20-30 variants instead of remaking ads from scratch, and hold your winning copy steady while you rotate creative.
