## Stop Being Broke. Get Busy.
`H_ZLs1-jOKQ` · https://youtu.be/H_ZLs1-jOKQ

*The case for deliberately doing the unscalable work when you're small — one-to-one onboarding, handwritten cards, phone sales below your ticket price — because the constraint is skill, not physics, and the unscalable version is the fastest way to learn the customer; then climb the done-for-you -> done-with-you -> do-it-yourself pyramid top-down.*

### Case study

**Business.** Autobiographical — his own businesses (fitness gyms, then the portfolio). Not a stranger's teardown. He also uses Andy Frisella's supplement company and an unnamed $100M+/year portfolio company as supporting cases.

**Starting state.** Starting a business with no context, no resources, no help and no money, where the unscalable approach looks unscalable precisely because of that lack of leverage. He describes the 'swamp': you don't have enough money to pay somebody else, so you work today's job and tomorrow's job simultaneously.

**Diagnosis.** The constraint is SKILL, not scalability. Nobody has proven that gravity stops outbound, handwritten cards or one-to-one onboarding from scaling — they've only shown they personally don't know how to hire and train their way out of it. The second diagnosis is sequencing: most new businesses start on the hardest-to-sell end of the sales-to-fulfillment continuum (do-it-yourself), which is backwards.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Do the unscalable work deliberately: one-to-one onboarding, phone calls on sales below your ticket price, handwritten cards, personal video and voice notes via iMessage from a personal phone.
- 2. Treat the low-ticket customer as paid education: 'you're learning more from them than you are earning from them'. Learn the pain points, the hooks that matter, and how to alter the offer to convert better.
- 3. Run the two magic questions on every customer to build a power ranking of features and to find the dead weight.
- 4. Convert one-to-one into one-to-six (6x output), build a presentation around the six recurring questions, then one-to-20 and one-to-30 (180 people/day with one person), then teach somebody else to run the same deck. That is the path from unscalable to scalable.
- 5. Extract the 20% of the unscalable process that drives 80% of the impact, add cash and leverage, and accept 80% of the effect at 10x the output.
- 6. Sequence products top-down (the Tesla model): most expensive done-for-you first, use it to develop the SOPs, then step down to done-with-you (1/3 to 1/5 the price) and DIY (1/10), selling 10x the people at a tenth of the handholding.

**Result.** Reported as the basis of his track record: 9 businesses founded and exited, the last at $46.2 million, current portfolio over $200 million a year. The sales skill that produced it came from 4,101 personal closes. A company still in the portfolio scaled to $100M+/year while deliberately keeping group onboarding.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Track record | **9 businesses; last exit $46.2M; portfolio $200M+/year** |
| Closes that produced his sales skill | **4,101 closes over multiple years** |
| Onboarding scale achieved | **one-on-30 = 180 people/day with one person; portfolio…** |
| Pyramid price steps | **$10,000/month private clients -> 1/3 to 1/5 -> 1/10** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When something in your business looks 'unscalable', the correct response is not to avoid it — it is to test whether it is physically impossible. If it isn't, the blocker is a skill you don't yet have, and the way to acquire the skill is to do the unscalable version now while you're small, because the unscalable version is also the fastest teacher (you learn more from the customer than you earn from them). Then convert it in stages: one-to-one -> one-to-six -> one-to-twenty -> one-to-thirty -> teach someone else the deck, extracting the 20% of the original that drove 80% of the impact and…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The 'unscalable' label is diagnosed here as a skill deficiency rather than a real constraint — 'it's unskill, not unscalable' — and the test is whether physics forbids it. That reframe is absent from the standard scaling material.
- The financial-debt vs management-debt framing (every business incurs one or the other; if you can't pay for talent you pay with your own hours working the jobs of 2-4 people) is a specific way of accounting for the cost of being small.
- The two magic questions (what would you keep if you could keep only one; what could I remove that would change nothing) are given as a repeatable feature-ranking procedure with a sample size (ask 100 people), not just 'get customer feedback'.
- The unscalable-to-scalable conversion path is stated as a concrete ladder: one-to-one -> one-to-six -> build a deck around the six recurring questions -> one-to-twenty/one-to-thirty -> teach someone the deck. With the extraction rule: keep the 20% of the unscalable process that drove 80% of the…
- The sales-to-fulfillment continuum is paired here with an explicit sequencing rule (start at the most expensive, hardest-to-fulfill end, i.e. top-down / 'the Tesla model') and a justification — least operational drag at the top because you have the fewest customers, plus you develop the SOPs on the…
- The context-contamination point — people give advice from their current setting to people not in that context, which is why he deliberately spends time with people at the $10K, $100K and $1M/month levels — is a caution about how his own published advice should be read.

## I Built 4 Businesses In A Row To Show It's Not Luck
`0mqqbuM9sAk` · https://youtu.be/0mqqbuM9sAk

*Case 1 of 4 — Gym Launch: a gym-owner licensing business built on Client Financed Acquisition (customers pay for the next customer's acquisition), scaling from $120k to $1M/month, peaking at a $150M valuation and selling for $46.2M after COVID.*

### Case study 1

**Business.** Gym Launch — a licensing business for gym owners. He had a working gym-growth model and licensed it to other gym owners, who used it to make more money.

**Starting state.** Zero customers, no list, no audience. First attempt at acquisition was a scraped CrossFit email list run through a Facebook lookalike audience to a webinar, which produced 80 opt-ins and zero sales or booked calls.

**Diagnosis.** Capital was the binding constraint on growth — which he solved structurally rather than by raising money: if the first sale pays for both the acquisition and the fulfillment of the current AND the next customer, you never need outside capital. The secondary diagnosis on product: the deliverable has to be exceptional, and the difference between good and great took six years to build.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Do the unscalable thing to get the first ten customers: manually find the 80 opt-in emails, friend them on Facebook, message them, and sell $500 in-person turnarounds.
- 2. Once the model was proven, switch to the licensing version — a product with virtually 100% margins — and simply sell more units each month.
- 3. Adopt Client Financed Acquisition as the growth model in every business thereafter: price and structure so the first transaction funds the acquisition and fulfillment of the next customer, eliminating capital as a constraint and allowing him to outspend competitors.
- 4. Product improvement loop: identify whatever problem clients currently have (churn, margin, lead flow, close rate), form a hypothesis, survey the community for who has the best numbers on that metric, invite 20 of them onto a call, take notes, and extract the FEW things they all did in common.
- 5. Frame every change to clients as worth the cost of change, with a demonstrated long-term benefit.

**Result.** Ramped from $120,000 in month one to $1M/month within a few months on unit sales alone. Peak valuation ~$150M. Hit by COVID (a third of all clients went out of business) and sold for $46.2M to American Pacific Group. Average client gym made an extra $100,000/year in profit and an extra $30,000 in cash in the first 30 days.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue ramp | **$120k -> $300k -> $400k+ -> $780k -> $1M/month** |
| Exit | **peak $150M, sold for $46.2M** |
| Client result | **+$30,000 cash in first 30 days on a $36,000/year profit base** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Fund growth out of the first transaction instead of raising capital. Structure the offer so that one sale covers the cost of acquiring AND fulfilling the current customer plus the cost of acquiring and fulfilling the next one — then capital is no longer the constraint and you can outspend everyone. Pair that with a disciplined product-improvement loop: pick the single metric you want to fix, find the clients who are already best at it, study the FEW things they all do in common (not everything they do), and ship that. And note the two failure modes he names: overhiring support (35 reps when 5…

### Case study 2

**Business.** Prestige Labs — a supplements company, structurally a sister company to Gym Launch, sold exclusively through the gym-owner affiliate base with direct-to-consumer shipping managed centrally.

**Starting state.** He had no intention of entering supplements. The trigger was a customer paying $700 for $400 of product he had recommended. He had an existing distribution base of gym owners from Gym Launch to sell through, but no product, no tech and no supply chain.

**Diagnosis.** The opportunity was an acquisition subsidy plus a distribution advantage: if every gym customer also bought supplements, the physical product margin would cover the cost of acquiring that customer, and there was no added fulfillment burden because shipping was centralised. The risks he identifies in hindsight are supply chain fragility (one missing ingredient blocks the whole product), predatory law firms (buying product to test, then suing once you have a patent and working on rev-share), and a fundamentally non-sticky end consumer in fitness.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Recruit gym owners and pitch supplements as the acquisition subsidy: sell every customer supplements and the physical product covers your CAC.
- 2. Build channel-specific infrastructure: a full point-of-sale for supplements made specifically for gyms, a retail kit (a full wall of products) and a kiosk with an iPad-style device per gym.
- 3. Keep the brand exclusive — only gym owners could sell it — and price the main site 30% higher so the gym price represents real savings.
- 4. Give the gym owners a strong selling system and make it a recurring subscription, so each customer generates two recurring subscriptions.
- 5. Roll out in waves: 10 locations first, then 20-30, then another 20-30, then the full launch.
- 6. Accept the capital cost: $4M to start, split roughly $1M tech and $3M product.

**Result.** $1.7 million in the first fully operational month. He nonetheless concludes: 'the biggest lesson... is that I probably shouldn't have done it' — Gym Launch stopped growing the year Prestige Labs launched, and he became CEO of two companies rather than one.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| First fully operational month | **$1.7M** |
| Startup capital | **$4M ($1M tech, ~$3M product)** |
| Price advantage for gym owners | **30% below the main site** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Attach a high-margin physical product to an existing distribution channel to subsidise customer acquisition — and then build channel-specific tooling (POS, kits, subscriptions) that generic competitors cannot or will not build, because that tooling is the moat. But the honest lesson is about attention: launching a second company while the first was still growing meant the first stopped growing, and he became the CEO of two companies instead of one. A new business is not free just because it is profitable — the cost is the growth you forgo in the business you already had.

### Case study 3

**Business.** Allen (useallen.com) — software that aggregates scheduling and appointment data across small brick-and-mortar businesses to predictively determine which days, times and follow-up sequences get the most people to show up.

**Starting state.** Built off the insight that if you aggregate all the scheduling data from every type of small in-person appointment business, you can predictively show what drives show-ups. He started it to solve the problem for gym owners, where 'people don't work their leads' was the biggest constraint. Sold initially into his existing distribution base.

**Diagnosis.** Two problems. (1) Distribution: they could not expand outside their own base, because small business owners who used the product immediately asked how to get leads — they were selling to the wrong level of the market. (2) Build quality: they used an external development shop (the same one that built the Prestige Labs software), which he now calls 'about as close to a complete scam as you can come to' — a software company needs an in-house CTO.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Pivot the customer up one level: sell to agencies rather than small businesses, because one agency carries ~50 small business owners and gives a whole extra degree of leverage.
- 2. Do two webinars to audiences of agency owners with big lists — one pitch reaching a thousand customers.
- 3. Run pricing surveys early and repackage how you charge (usage-based, recurring fees, different APIs) — this unlocked 4x pricing power.
- 4. Align incentives with the customer by charging on show-ups, which makes every stakeholder want the same outcome.
- 5. Fix appointment throughput for clients: more days open, more hours, smaller time increments, more availability and flexibility.

**Result.** $12 million in the trailing 12 months before sale. Sold 75% to a strategic buyer in an all-stock deal (value under NDA); the buyer still runs it. Within 6 months of the agency pivot they were doing $1.7M/month through the software company.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| T12M revenue before sale | **$12M** |
| Show rate improvement | **9% -> just under 20%** |
| Agency pivot result | **$1.7M/month within 6 months** |
| Pricing power | **4x from repackaging** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When a product works but distribution stalls, move one level up the value chain rather than sideways: sell to the people who already own the customer relationship (agencies), because one sale there carries dozens of end customers and the marketing effort per customer collapses. Then, for software specifically, two rules: never outsource the build (an external dev shop is the equivalent of white-labelling your delivery — build an in-house engineering capability), and run pricing surveys early because how you charge (usage, recurring, API tiers) can be worth multiples of what you charge.…

### Case study 4

**Business.** Acquisition.com — a portfolio of companies (also a private equity-style investor) that does over $200M/year, built as a capital compounding vehicle on his personal brand, book, videos and podcast.

**Starting state.** Starting from a question rather than an opportunity: what could I do forever, worked backwards from there. Requirements were high leverage and a capital compounding vehicle. The first 10 investments came from people he already knew whose relationships had already become advisory.

**Diagnosis.** The design problem was leverage and permanence, not a specific market gap. Operationally, the constraint on speed is talent, and the biggest cost in any business is what you do not know.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Build on a personal brand and inbound content rather than outbound — accepting a slower, more selective funnel in exchange for pre-aligned prospects.
- 2. Source deals from the audience (book readers, video watchers, podcast listeners) plus his existing network, taking $3M+ businesses, mostly over $5M, averaging $17M.
- 3. Hire top-down from day one: director of sales, director of marketing, director of people, director of IT, director of portfolio operations — people better than him at their function who could teach him.
- 4. Be the bank: deliberately pay down financial debt so as not to carry management, cultural or technical debt later.
- 5. Make recruiting talent the core competency of the business, using inbound volume, PE prestige and a Holdco training layer to place and onboard managers into portfolio companies.
- 6. Cross-pollinate: co-own businesses across industries so that what works in one can be transplanted into another.

**Result.** Portfolio does over $200M/year. Average portfolio business does $17M. He reports learning more than ever because he is exposed to more businesses at a higher level, and that the top-down hiring model is the one he will use from here on out.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Portfolio revenue | **$200M+/year** |
| Deal criteria | **$3M+ minimum, most over $5M, average $17M** |
| Biggest cost in a business | **what you do not know** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Design the business backwards from 'what could I do forever' and choose the structure that maximises leverage and compounding rather than the one that is fastest to start. Then decide which kind of debt you are willing to carry: every business carries one of financial, management, cultural or technical debt, and being well capitalised early (being your own bank) is a deliberate trade to avoid paying down the other three later. Hire top-down from day one if you can afford it — directors who are better than you at their function, who can teach you — because that is what allows you to delegate…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- Client Financed Acquisition is the most portable framework in this video and is usually summarised as 'make money on the front end'; the actual test is arithmetic — first sale must cover acquisition + fulfillment of the current AND the next customer.
- The product-improvement loop is stated with a sample-size rule (invite the top 20, look for the few things ALL of them do) rather than generic 'study your best customers'.
- He explicitly warns that a spectacular return on marketing can be an artefact of timing arbitrage, which the published case-study material rarely admits.
- The strategic point here is unusual and worth preserving: a profitable new business can still be a net negative if it stops the growth of the existing one — the cost is opportunity, not cash.
- The moat argument is made through channel-specific tooling (POS, retail kits, kiosks, selling systems, subscriptions) rather than brand or product quality, which is a different moat theory than the standard material.
- He names three structural risks of physical products that the general offer material omits: supply chain single-points-of-failure, predatory law firms (buy-and-test then rev-share litigation once you hold a patent), and a non-sticky end consumer in fitness.

## "I'm Broke... What Should I Do?"
`KNl83INePXI` · https://youtu.be/KNl83INePXI

*The answer to 'I'm dead broke, what do I do?' is skills — the only asset nobody can take from you — and the practical route to acquire them with money you already have is to buy an existing cash-flowing business from a motivated seller on seller financing, using the mentor-taught sequence 'agree on price, then agree on terms'.*

### Case study

**Business.** The fifth gym location — a gym acquired from a distressed owner (he also frames the wider answer around the two-scenario house-vs-business comparison and his own first and second gym buildouts).

**Starting state.** He already had four locations, the first built for about $40,000 (a former gym, so turf, flooring and paint already existed) and the second for $250,000 — which made no more money than the first. He had no spare capital to deploy for the fifth.

**Diagnosis.** Two diagnoses. (1) Capital is not the constraint — skill is, and skills are the only asset that cannot be confiscated. (2) The correct way to use the little money you have is not to start something from scratch but to buy an existing cash-flowing business from a motivated seller, because you inherit the book of business, client list, equipment, permits and licences, and you can make the asset finance itself. A business acquired this way can be bought with the same $50,000 that would otherwise be a house down payment, and it upgrades your income from $60,000 to $250,000.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Use the mentor-taught sequence: agree on price FIRST, then agree on terms. Never negotiate both at once.
- 2. On terms, ask the seller to sell-or-finance three quarters of the deal and push the payment period out as far as you can (he tried for 24 months; the seller agreed to 12).
- 3. Finance the remaining quarter with a bank or SBA loan, putting down as little as possible (in the worked example, $50,000 against a $200,000 loan — 25%).
- 4. Look for motivated sellers: owners who are done, or whose life circumstances (divorce, family crisis) force an exit. Do not wait for listed deals — reach out to brokers to learn local price ranges, but expect to pay retail if you buy through a broker.
- 5. Be patient enough to take six months. Impatience is what makes new buyers overpay.

**Result.** He agreed $40,000 on the fifth gym, paid nothing out of pocket, and did $51,000 in sales in the first 30 days — the gym paid for itself inside a month. It then threw off profit every month, and he sold it about 12 months later for 1.5x what he bought it for, having had the gym pay for itself. That deal is also how he met Russell and started teaching other gym owners.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Acquisition price | **$40,000** |
| Terms | **12 months seller financed, nothing down** |
| First 30 days | **$51,000 in sales — paid for itself** |
| Exit | **1.5x the purchase price** |
| Buildout comparison | **$40,000 (gym 1) vs $250,000 (gym 2) for the same output** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Two things to copy. First, the negotiation sequence: agree on PRICE first and TERMS second — never together — and on terms, ask the seller to carry three quarters of the deal over as long a period as they will accept, financing the rest with a bank loan against as little down as possible. That is how an asset with no money down still becomes yours. Second, the acquisition target: instead of starting from scratch, hunt for a business with a motivated seller (owner is done, or a life event forces an exit) and buy the existing book of business, client list, equipment, permits and licences rather…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- This is an older video (all-lowercase auto-captions, no punctuation) — his delivery style and the business context (gyms, Gym Launch-era) differ from the newer teardowns, which is worth flagging when the knowledge base compares advice across years.
- The 'agree on price, then agree on terms' sequence is attributed to an early mentor and presented as the tactic he has used his entire career — it is a distinct, named negotiation procedure not covered in the standard offer material.
- The concrete acquisition structure is quantified: 2.5x earnings multiple for a small local business doing $250,000/year profit, three quarters seller financed, one quarter bank-financed with 25% down, asset paying for itself inside 30 days.
- The risk-asymmetry observation is stated as an empirical claim about people he has been around at different wealth levels: wealthier people spend less, have lower risk tolerances, and buy things that cannot go to zero, for zero.
- He is candid that the numbers in the worked example are being calculated live and hedged ('i'm doing some math today but like 400 and you know 30-ish 437 whatever thousand dollars'), and that he does not remember whether first-house down payments are 10% or 20% — the transcript should be read with…

## How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]
`bgmh7p1s7zs` · https://youtu.be/bgmh7p1s7zs

*The operating manual for a consistent sales team: the Closer Framework (script built ONLY from questions, in six buckets, with three 30-second illustrative stories) plus the Five C's of managing reps — Closer, Call recordings, Comms, Cut the bottom 10%, Competition.*

### Case study

**Business.** His own sales organisation — built across his gyms and an outsourced sales company that flew reps out to fill other people's gyms, and the system he used to scale it past 20 people (he also names Marcus as the source of the five-C mnemonic).

**Starting state.** He was selling one-on-one himself — 4,000 closes, mostly weight loss, often in chaotic conditions. The teams he then ran suffered the standard symptoms he asks the room about: inconsistent lead quality, inconsistent CAC, reps who swing between underworked and overworked, and complaints about lead volume and efficiency.

**Diagnosis.** Two separate failure points. (1) The conversation is unmanaged: reps are given paragraphs and statements to read, which they cannot think through, so the script is not scalable and the close is inconsistent. (2) The team is unmanaged: no recordings, no cadence, no pruning and no competitive pressure, so performance decays and nobody knows where calls are failing. Cutting the bottom of the team is named as the single biggest lever on performance.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Rebuild the script as questions only. Nothing in the framework may be a paragraph or a statement, because a rep can pause and ask another question with no intelligence required — which is what makes it scalable.
- 2. Structure the script as buckets: Clarify (what made you get on the call, what's your goal, why is that important, what would it look like 12 months from now), Label (name their problem back to them and get agreement), Overview the pain (the pain cycle, run until they have nothing left, then…
- 3. Walk them through the decision in yes/no steps and make them confront it — including asking what card they want to use.
- 4. Record every call (compliance + accountability) and review them; he names Gong as the tool.
- 5. Set the comms cadence: daily huddles to share testimonials, weekly one-on-ones where the rep tags you in their best, worst and average call and shows you where they clarified the pain and asked for the sale, plus monthly.
- 6. Cut the bottom 10% regularly — even when the team is going okay, because it produces a 30% productivity jump every time.
- 7. Publish a daily leaderboard with notifications on every sale, and run 6-week prize competitions in 3-person teams at roughly 25% of one month's cheque per head.

**Result.** A 20+ person sales team running on the Closer Framework plus the Five C's, producing what he describes as wicked consistent sales on a monthly basis. His outsourced sales operation filled gyms in 30 days by flying reps out to sell for them. He personally closed 4,000 people one-on-one.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| His personal closing volume | **4,000 one-on-one closes** |
| Outsourced sales result | **gyms filled in 30 days** |
| Effect of cutting the bottom | **30% productivity jump every time** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Copy two things. First, the script construction rule: every line of your sales framework must be a QUESTION, never a statement or a paragraph — the test is whether a rep can deliver it while pausing and asking a follow-up, which is exactly what makes it trainable and scalable. Structure it as six buckets (Clarify, Label, Overview the pain, Sell the vacation, Explain away concerns, Reinforce the decision) and give reps only three 30-second illustrative stories to memorise, one per component of the outcome they're selling. Second, the management layer: record every call, run daily huddles…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- This is a conference-talk recording rather than a teardown of a named stranger's business — the case study is his own sales organisation, and the value is the process detail rather than a revenue result.
- The rule that the script must contain ONLY questions (no statements or paragraphs) is stated with its reason — a rep can pause and ask a follow-up without needing intelligence, which is what makes it scalable — a construction constraint not spelled out in the general closing material.
- The Closer Framework is given as six ordered buckets with sample wording for each (Clarify, Label, Overview, Sell the vacation, Explain away concerns, Reinforce the decision), plus the explicit claim that there are only three objections: price, stall, decision-maker.
- The management system is quantified: cut the bottom 10% on a regular basis for a 30% productivity jump; 6-week competitions; 3-person teams; prize budget of ~25% of one month's cheque per person.
- The prize-budget example is garbled in the caption ('if your guys make 70, you might spend 1,500 bucks') — the salary unit is lost, so the $1,500 and $5,000 figures should be treated as illustrative rather than derived.
- He names Gong specifically as the call-recording tool for Zoom-based sales, and states that recording is also a compliance requirement, not just a coaching tool.

## I Built My $100M Business WRONG...
`sKCrYIWPHLc` · https://youtu.be/sKCrYIWPHLc

*Four lessons from sitting in a room with eight entrepreneurs doing $500M+/year combined, where he was the second smallest: Scale Zero (drive your own requirement to zero before you scale), go after an ocean instead of a lake, run one primary business vehicle (because to decide is to kill off the alternatives), and sell something with both high margin AND high value.*

### Case study

**Business.** His own portfolio (Acquisition.com and the businesses behind the '$100 million in a single niche') — self-teardown against the benchmark of seven peers in a '$500 million dollar mastermind'.

**Starting state.** Second smallest in a room of eight entrepreneurs doing $500M+/year combined, finishing the year at ~$32M. He was running three businesses as CEO of all of them, splitting his attention, and was personally doing work inside the businesses — 20 hours a week that would become 40 if the business doubled. He had generated $100M in a single niche (gyms) and had niching down as an advantage, not a limitation, at that stage.

**Diagnosis.** Four diagnosed errors, each visible by contrast with the bigger operators in the room. (1) He was the bottleneck — the business still required him, so scaling would multiply his workload rather than free it. (2) He was in a lake, not an ocean: everyone bigger was going after a bigger marketplace. (3) He had three businesses and was CEO of all of them, while everyone else had one business and one customer — costing him an estimated two years of development. (4) His margin structure was worse than the room's; the two lowest-margin operators in the room were the smallest businesses.

**Intervention.**

- 1. Adopt Scale Zero as the target state: drive the business to literally zero requirement of him, deliberately becoming less important to the company's success so it can grow without him. Accept that this is hard, that you fail a lot, that you hire people who mess up and you eat the cost of those…
- 2. Walk the outsourcing ladder: do everything, then outsource admin, then back-end customer service, then sales, then marketing, then the messaging behind the overarching market position — until the only thing left is making the biggest and most important decisions.
- 3. Move from lake to ocean: go after a bigger marketplace rather than staying in the niche that made him successful (while acknowledging that starting in a lake is the right call when you're starting out).
- 4. Consolidate to one primary vehicle and one customer, and kill off the alternatives — 'to decide is to kill off'. If owning pieces of multiple businesses, do it as an owner with a hired CEO and equity-incentivised executive team, not as an active partner.
- 5. Target high margin AND high value rather than high margin with low value.
- 6. Hire pre-loaded operators ('batteries included') who have already done the thing, rather than teaching someone — and build toward a structure of better decision-making leaders so he is not the bottleneck.

**Result.** Stated as lessons being applied going forward rather than a completed turnaround: he estimates the multi-business period cost him about two years of development, has developed a skill set that now spans 100+ niches through agencies, and frames the four constraints (ocean, one thing, high margin + high value, structured so he is not the bottleneck) as the filter for his next moves.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| His revenue relative to the room | **~$32M, second smallest of eight doing $500M+ combined** |
| Cost of running three businesses | **~2 years of development lost** |
| The bottleneck arithmetic | **20 hrs/week -> 40 hrs/week on a doubling** |
| Margin correlation observed | **everyone but one sold high gross margin; the two…** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Run these four checks against your own business, in this order. (1) Scale Zero: can the business grow without you, or does doubling it double your workload? If the latter, the job is to make yourself less important — walk the outsourcing ladder from admin to customer service to sales to marketing to positioning, until the only thing left for you is the biggest decisions. Expect to eat the cost of other people's mistakes as tuition. (2) Ocean vs lake: the niche that made you successful is not the market you should scale in once you have the skill set — lakes are right for starting, oceans are…

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- This is a lessons/reflection video, not a teardown of a stranger's business — the case study is his own portfolio benchmarked against seven peers, and there is no before/after revenue intervention to report.
- Scale Zero is stated as an absolute ('literally zero requirement of me... not like eat like zero none') with the arithmetic that makes it necessary (20 hrs/week doubles to 40), and is paired with an explicit outsourcing ladder and an honest statement of the cost: you fail a lot, hire people who…
- The 'oceans not lakes' lesson comes with a stage caveat that is easy to lose when quoting it — niching down to a lake was the correct call for him at the time, and the ocean advice applies to his current season only. He says so explicitly twice.
- The 'decide = kill off' etymology is a memorable device for enforcing focus, and it is paired with the correct model for owning multiple businesses: hired CEO, equity-incentivised executive team, owner advises strategically rather than operating.
- The margin observation is a correlation within one specific room of eight people (the two lowest-margin operators were the smallest businesses, everyone else sold high gross margin), not a measured causal claim — worth preserving as an observation rather than a law.
- The cost of the multi-business period is quantified as an estimated two years of entrepreneurial development lost — his own retrospective estimate.

## STEAL Ryan Reynolds' $1.3B Marketing Strategy [NO FAME REQUIRED]
`HwPXctiw_rY` · https://youtu.be/HwPXctiw_rY

*A frame-by-frame teardown of Mint Mobile's winning and losing paid ads - contrarian hooks, us-versus-them, reverse value equation, levels of awareness, offer re-wrapping, three-tier pricing - plus the landing page, sales page and email sequence behind them.*

### Case study

**Business.** Mint Mobile - budget wireless carrier owned/represented by Ryan Reynolds, selling SIM-only unlimited plans online

**Starting state.** Over 2 million customers acquired through paid ads; single price point of $15/month for the first three months ($45 up front) with the offer re-wrapped seasonally; traffic all pushed to one landing page

**Diagnosis.** Mint is an underdog fighting Verizon and AT&T, so its winning theme is us-versus-them built on price; its winning creative is a recognized spokesperson plus humour, and its funnel problem is congruence and objection coverage rather than awareness

**Intervention.**

- Run a contrarian hook that sets up us-versus-them (we do the opposite of what big wireless does)
- Deliver value as 'we deflate prices due to not hating you' and close on a joke rather than a happy customer
- Keep the winning offer identical and change only the wrapper (holiday promo, New Year promo, stock-footage promo)
- Run two creative categories: produced brand ads with the celebrity and native UGC ads from creators and customers
- Target most-aware audiences with a bare offer (buy three get three) and reserve curiosity hooks for cold traffic
- Push all traffic to one landing page with a ZIP coverage checker, then a plan selector with a dummy middle tier, then a sales page with FAQ and a nurture capture
- Follow up by email, one objection per email in order of prevalence

**Result.** The teardown identifies which ads are working by runtime - the oldest ad has run 5-6 years and is judged to be a retargeting campaign; the chunky-milk ad is judged a failure because it branded against its own product and removed the star

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Customers acquired through paid ads | **over 2 million** |
| Headline price and upfront cash | **$15/month for three months, $45 up front** |
| Runtime of the oldest ad found in the Facebook Ads Library | **5 or 6 years** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Copy the structure, not the fame: contrarian hook, us-versus-them (or us-versus-the-alternative if you lead), value as more-good/less-bad plus the 'don't', a recognized spokesperson or native UGC, one winning offer re-wrapped endlessly, and a funnel that answers objections in the order they appear.

## Your Business Is NOT What You Think It Is
`rj7rzOdj84A` · https://youtu.be/rj7rzOdj84A

*A single continuous argument: the business you think you are in is not the business you are in, the difference is a 'big hairy problem' you must name, and push-or-pivot is decided by whether your first-principles assumptions have been proven wrong.*

### Case study

**Business.** Airbnb cleaning company started by an existing Gym Launch gym owner (third party, unnamed)

**Starting state.** Started as self-cleaning of his own Airbnbs to protect margin, then extended to other people's Airbnbs. By the time Hormozi had dinner with him the business had been running about a year, had CAC of about $6 and, in his words, insane LTV because people never cancel. He was not making gazillions because of one constraint: talent - getting cleaners who show up on time, do a good job, don't steal, speak English and communicate with customers.

**Diagnosis.** He was not in the marketing and sales business the way he was in his gyms, because selling house cleaning is easy and getting people to opt in to cleaning ads is not hard. The hard part is delivering, and there are no 'cleaning enthusiasts' the way there are fitness enthusiasts, so the scarce input is labour. Hormozi's read: 'you're in the recruiting and training business.'

**Intervention.** Flip the customer funnel into a talent funnel: acquisition becomes generating leads and applications for talent, sales calls become interviews, customer onboarding becomes new-employee onboarding and training, and management becomes the retention mechanism that ascends people up inside the organisation.

**Result.** Hormozi says he took the business from roughly $30,000-$40,000 a month to over $150,000 a month within the next 12 months.

## If I Wanted To Scale A Service Business In 2026, Here's What I'd Do
`N5MExtki_VI` · https://youtu.be/N5MExtki_VI

*Live teardown of Couplepreneurs (Kyle and Ariel, $480K/yr): he identifies a supply constraint disguised as a product problem, collapses two offers into one $25K/$30K offer delivered one-on-four, and converts the five-day challenge into a four-hour 'date night' so twice as many people get pitched.*

### Case study

**Business.** Couplepreneurs - Kyle and Ariel coach entrepreneur couples (couples who run businesses together or each own one) via a 12-month Rise Together Mentorship and a 12-month high-touch Couplepreneur Accelerator, plus annual live events.

**Starting state.** About $480,000 revenue and $206,000 profit over the last 12 months (43% margin), a setter, a customer-service person, 42 active couples, 4 clients lost in 12 months. Three stated problems: a cash-flow cycle where it can take months to recoup acquisition spend, declining challenge attendance, and their own time being maxed out by customization. Cost per average attendee $815; attendee show-up rate 5.25%.

**Diagnosis.** The real constraint was supply, not product. They had given unlimited Slack access to themselves, which took ~40% of their time, then built a second low-touch product instead of removing the time demand from the first - so the customer's cost for the low-touch thing equalled the high-touch thing and the economics stopped working. The highest-value deliverable (the in-person events) was the thing nobody was paying for directly, and the least-loved deliverable (weekly group calls) was bundled in.

**Intervention.**

- Collapse the two offers into one: $25K paid in full / $30K on a payment plan (was 25K), delivered one-on-four quarterly instead of one-on-one, plus one one-on-one deep-dive onboarding and two in-person events per year.
- Eliminate Slack entirely and replace it with a capped number of '911 calls' (two to four) on an escalation basis.
- Cut the weekly group calls (surveyed as clients' least favourite) and let the events plus quarterly deep dives carry delivery; delivery drops to roughly 10 hours per couple.
- Price/cash: take the quarter up front - 9K down - and start payments of $2,500-$3,000/month immediately; downsell layaway (three payments then start).
- Convert the five-day challenge into a four-hour 'date night' run on a Friday, pitched at the end - roughly 3 hours of quality content out of the 5, so twice as many people hear the pitch.
- Add a $2,500 rebate for clients who film their first date night and grant usage rights, and feed that footage into ads.
- Move to daily organic content (from ~2/week), slice the best clips with a 5-second CTA for ads, and run ~100 static images instead of 12-16.
- Only ascend on renewal: sunset the low-ticket offer, do renewals in person at events with a fast-action bonus (first-class tickets worth ~$6,000 or $5,000 off).

**Result.** Forward-looking: he models 120 clients at two days a week of delivery = about $3 million, and a reverse-engineered 150 clients at ~$30K = $4.5 million, 10x current earnings. Stated multipliers: 5x on price already, 1-4x from the date-night angle, 1.5-2x from organic/CAC reduction.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Starting revenue and profit | **$480K revenue / $206K profit / 43% margin** |
| Modelled outcome at two delivery days a week | **120 clients, about $3 million** |
| Reverse-engineered target outcome | **150 clients at ~$30K = $4.5M** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When you are supply constrained, do not build a second product - remove the delivery that consumes you and change the ratio (1:1 -> 1:4). Price the remaining offer on the value of the one thing customers actually love (here, the in-person events), cap access instead of granting it unlimited, pull cash forward with a quarter-up-front plus layaway downsell, and turn the front-end event into a shorter single-session format that pitches twice as many people.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The caption renders the rebate price as '32.5' with no unit ('So, it's like it's 32.5, but you get $2,500 back') - the dollar figure and scale are only inferable from context, so it is recorded as stated.
- Their stated show-up rate on day one (9%) and the ad-data figure (5.25%) are both in the transcript and do not reconcile; the transcript gives no explanation.

## The Mathematics of Business, Explained

## I Reverse Engineered the Perfect Business
`HKbFUWJwEG0` · https://youtu.be/HKbFUWJwEG0

*The ten components of Enterprise Value — taught as the pieces of a masterpiece painting — where a business is worth customers times lifetime gross profit divided by risk, and each of the ten fixes lowers risk so the multiple goes up.*

### Case study

**Business.** A brick-and-mortar chain in the acquisition.com portfolio that had plateaued and needed a professional operator

**Starting state.** The business had plateaued at a point where the two founders could no longer carry it; growth had stalled and the partners identified that a more seasoned operator was required

**Diagnosis.** The constraint was founder-dependence in leadership — the business could not grow or be sold while the founders were the reason it existed, which meant no institutional buyer would take it

**Intervention.**

- Brought in an operator with a track record of taking a brick-and-mortar chain from 100 to 2,000 locations over more than ten years
- Transferred day-to-day leadership of the business to him
- Rather than pushing new openings, he proposed spending an entire quarter focused solely on making all existing locations more profitable

**Result.** The business continued to grow at the same pace while profitability expanded at a dramatically faster rate; the demonstrated operator removed the key-man risk, which is what made the business attractive to a future buyer

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Operator's prior track record | **100 to 2,000 locations over 10+ years** |
| The contrasting outcome in the same portfolio | **nine months not profitable** |

> **Transferable pattern.** A business is only worth what it is worth without you in it, so the first thing to buy is an operator who has already done the specific thing your business needs at a larger scale — not the person who is available, loyal or cheap. Track record on a comparable problem is the predictor; and the operator's first act can legitimately be improving the profitability of what already exists rather than opening more.

## I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here's how]
`pWbSl7d0tEc` · https://youtu.be/pWbSl7d0tEc

*A step-by-step walkthrough of the institutional sale process — prerequisites that kill deals, choosing and negotiating with a banker, the 500-buyer marketing funnel, and the purchase-agreement terms that decide how much of the headline number you actually keep.*

### Case study

**Business.** Gym Launch (and the 2021 sale of two companies to APG for $46.2 million)

**Starting state.** A guru-style business where the founder was the key man — the rainmaker and the face of fulfilment, which meant the business had key-man risk and would be worth little to an institutional buyer if he left

**Diagnosis.** The binding constraint was key-man risk plus the absence of a defined, repeatable acquisition process — the two prerequisites that most commonly kill institutional deals. He also cites single-channel dependence as a risk he had to solve when paid ads stopped performing during the pandemic

**Intervention.**

- Took three to five years to systematically remove key-man risk, converting the business from a guru business into a licensing business at enterprise level
- Hired one person to build an outbound department from scratch, giving a third acquisition channel alongside inbound
- Declared upfront to all parties that the exit would be a full leadership exit with no seller financing, no earn-out, no transition services and no consulting, with real equity and a sale of 66
- Negotiated the right to disclose the price into the sale agreement
- Ran the full institutional process: banker search, CIM, teaser to 500 buyers, about 98 NDAs, about 14 or 15 management presentations, two to four LOIs, negotiated against each other, exclusive LOI, 60-90 days of diligence, purchase agreement, escrow release

**Result.** Two companies sold in 2021 for $46.2 million, with the closing shown on camera and referred to as a $50 million deal; the buyer spent about $1 million on diligence and the escrow released in a 90-day and a one-year tranche

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| 2021 sale price | **$46.2 million for two companies** |
| Buyer's diligence spend | **about $1 million** |
| Time to remove key-man risk | **three to five years** |
| Structure he insisted on | **no seller financing, no earn-out, no transition services,…** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Remove key-man risk years before you want to sell, not during the sale — a business whose customers come for the founder has no enterprise value, and fixing it is a three-to-five-year project. Then declare your non-negotiables (cash versus paper, involvement, transition) to every party upfront so the bankers negotiate the points you actually care about, and be willing to walk away, because the buyer negotiates for a living and you do not.

> **Transferable pattern.** Value a hire by the annual gross profit they produce, then set your recruiting spend as a small fraction of that asset's price — the same logic he applies to paying $100M-level compensation for elite AI talent. ## If I Had To Start a Business From Scratch, I'd Do This
`HsQeQM1jUeg` · https://youtu.be/HsQeQM1jUeg

*A chronological walkthrough of the four stages he actually used to get his first 10 customers — free training for friends, referrals, a charity-donation free project, then a $200/month paid program — followed by what he did right, what he did wrong, and the 13 directions he now gives to beginners.*

### Case study

**Business.** His own first online coaching business — personal training and nutrition coaching, starting as the 'Free Training Project' and monetising as 'Skinny to Swole'

**Starting state.** A consultant in Baltimore with no clients, no proof, no offer and no sales process; working out himself and competing on a local powerlifting team

**Diagnosis.** He had skill and no proof, so the constraint was credibility — and later, once money was coming in, no ascension offer, no sales process and no pricing power.

**Intervention.**

- Stage 1 (6 months): train friends free in exchange for before-and-after photos and testimonials
- Stage 2: ask the free clients for referrals (got 6–10, but almost none engaged because it was free)
- Stage 3: the Free Training Project — referrals donate $500–$1,000 to a charity of their choice, creating skin in the game while he still took no money
- Build a templated deliverable: a 200-hour Excel sheet generating macros and grocery lists across 100 meals, delivered in ~10 minutes per client
- Stage 4: launch Skinny to Swole at $200/month for 12 weeks and transfer the free clients across without losing many
- Post his first-ever advertising post (a personal story plus transformation images plus 'I have a few slots open') and text the link to everyone he knew

**Result.** First 20 paying clients at $200/month = $4,000/month, $12,000 over the 12 weeks — matching his consulting income on his first attempt.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| First paid cohort revenue | **20 clients × $200/month = $4,000/month, $12,000 over 12…** |
| Time invested in stage one | **six months** |
| Referrals from the free cohort | **6 to 10** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Sequence credibility before cash: give it away free to people who already like you until you have proof, convert the proof into referrals, then add a non-monetary cost to create commitment, then charge — and build the templated deliverable during the free period so the paid version costs you almost nothing to deliver. The named failure to avoid is having no ascension offer and no sales conversation once the first cohort buys.

## Watch this to keep more customers
`afbP6sB_Atc` · https://youtu.be/afbP6sB_Atc

*A six-month teardown of a portfolio SaaS company: fix onboarding first, then reset expectations in the sales script, then align CS incentives — producing a 61% drop in cancellations, 48% ascension, and 2.4x companywide upsells.*

### Case study

**Business.** A SaaS portfolio company at acquisition.com — software sold and onboarded through live one-to-many calls to roughly 25 new customers per call, with a sales team, a customer-success team and an upsell/ascension path.

**Starting state.** The software had been implemented in the business 90 days earlier. Churn spiked, customer satisfaction scores fell, and the number of people taking the next upsell dropped. Hormozi's stated goal was to save $2 million in bottom-line profit in 6 months.

**Diagnosis.** Three problem areas, in the order he found them: (1) onboarding — one-to-many calls with too much company-wide content, a third of the call spent resetting passwords, a hard pitch at the end and no defined next steps; (2) expectations set by sales that the product could not meet ('too techy', 'not enough support', 'not fast enough'); (3) misaligned incentives — the sales team fielding support calls, an unmotivated customer-success team, and unstructured, unpractised cancellation calls.

**Intervention.**

- Fix onboarding first, because the first impression forms in the first 24-48 hours post purchase and onboarding can add 2-3 months to LTV
- Pilot the changes on 15% of new customers rather than the whole business
- Move from one-to-many onboarding calls to one-to-one calls
- Apply the Closer framework's final R — reinforce the decision — with clarify, label and overview, and restate the customer's own stated goal back to them
- Give a quick win on the call (log in, take the tour) and connect the customer to support live while they are on the phone
- Rescript the sales process to set accurate expectations, which solved both the 'too techy' and 'not fast enough' complaints without changing close rates
- Increase the perception of support by making it more accessible (an in-app chat bubble) and use the support data to fix the single page generating 82% of complaints
- Lower the reading grade level of the product's language
- Create a dedicated escalations team to triage cancellation calls
- Align incentives: 10-15% commission on saves, so a rep is happy to spend $200 to keep a $2,000 sale
- Script and practise the customer-success conversations
- Run escalating outreach to cancelling customers — the inverse of lead nurture, following the bow-tie shape of the customer journey

**Result.** Onboarding ascensions went from 20% to 48%. Net change across the company: a 61% reduction in cancellations, 25% of people who got on a support/escalation call chose to ascend (one in four), and 2.4x the overall companywide ascensions. Hormozi states the headline outcome as saving $2 million in bottom-line profit in 6 months.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Stated headline outcome of the engagement | **$2 million in bottom-line profit, in 6 months** |
| Ascension rate from onboarding before and after the intervention | **20% → 48%** |
| Reduction in cancellations after all interventions | **61%** |
| Companywide ascension increase after all interventions | **2.4x** |
| Share of people who took an escalation/support call and chose to ascend | **25%, one in four** |
| Share of complaints traced to a single point in the product | **82%** |

> **Transferable pattern.** Fix onboarding before you fix anything downstream, because the first impression forms within 24-48 hours of purchase. Pilot changes on a slice (15%) rather than the whole customer base. Reinforce the buying decision immediately after purchase by restating the customer's own stated goal back to them. When customers say the product is 'too techy' or 'not fast enough', that is the inverse of the value equation — fix the sales script, not the product. Align the support team's incentives with saving the customer, not with fielding the call. Track the numbers or you will not care about them.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The '2.4x the overall ascensions' figure and the '20% to 48%' figure describe overlapping changes (the onboarding rebuild is described as producing the 20→48 move and also as a piece of the 2.4x aggregate), so the two should not be multiplied or added.
- The $2 million figure is explicitly the reduction/saving only; he says he deliberately excluded the additional revenue from the fixes, so total value is higher but unquantified.
- 'Allen' in the caption is his software company ALAN; the onboarding-language experiment (goal restatement doubling or tripling follow-through) is from that company, not from the portfolio SaaS business in the case study.
- He says he 'can't remember the number' for the ALAN follow-through multiple — 'doubled or tripled' is his own uncertainty, not a measured range.

## GROWTH LEVERS: Big Business Owner Explains Real World Tactics That Work
`F3NyhOtRpOE` · https://youtu.be/F3NyhOtRpOE

*A live 2022 event presentation of the $100M Offers framework — why the offer is the fastest shortcut to material success, the four things he looks at in any business (commodity problem, right avatar, premium price, value equation), and the worked teardown of an agency offer that went from $5,000 to $112,000 on the same ad spend.*

### Case study

**Business.** A brick-and-mortar marketing agency selling to local businesses (chiropractors and similar), sold through ALAN — the software company Hormozi's group later sold. Offer at the time: a $1,500/month retainer with a results-based promise.

**Starting state.** The offer was fully commoditised — 'pay me every month and either you get results or you don't' — with everyone in the group running more or less the same thing. The average agency in the group was getting about a 0.5-to-1 return on ad spend in the first 30 days: spend $1,000, make $500, then $1,000 the next month. They roughly broke even or lost slightly on the front end and made it up on the back end.

**Diagnosis.** The commodity problem. Because every agency sold the same thing, buyers made a price-based decision rather than a values-based one, which suppressed response rate, appointment volume, close rate and the price they could charge.

**Intervention.**

- Replace the monthly retainer with a one-time setup payment plus a pay-per-show model
- Charge once today to set everything up, then charge nothing again until someone physically walks into the client's business
- Wrap it in a continuity program carrying what he calls an implied guarantee

**Result.** On the same $10,000 of ad spend: response rate up 2.5x, appointments booked up from 40 to 100, shows up from 30 to 75, close rate up from 16% to 37% (2.3x), clients closed up from 5 to 28, and the price charged up 4x — producing $112,000 collected instead of $5,000. A 22.4x increase in cash collected upfront, and 0.5 to 11.2 on return on ad spend, with no change to creative, funnels or nurture sequences.

**Numbers.**

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| Return on ad spend for the average agency on the old offer | **about 0.5 to 1 in the first 30 days** |
| Old offer performance on $10,000 of ad spend | **300,000 reached; 0.13% response; 40 appointments; 30 shows;…** |
| New offer performance on the same $10,000 of ad spend | **100 appointments; 75 shows; 37% close; 28 closed; 4x price;…** |
| Headline result of the offer change | **22.4x increase in cash collected upfront ($5,000 → $112,000)** |
| Return on ad spend before and after, stated as a ratio | **0.5 → 11.2** |
| The change produced without touching the marketing machinery | **creative, funnels and nurture sequences all unchanged** |

> **Transferable pattern.** When an offer is commoditised, do not touch the creative or the funnel — change what you are offering. Restructure the payment to align with the buyer's definition of a result (pay-per-show instead of a retainer) so the buyer's risk drops without your price dropping. Removing the monthly commitment raises close rate and allows a higher price at the same time, because the buyer is now making a values-based rather than price-based decision. Measure the whole chain — reach, response, appointments, shows, close rate, price — because the compounding is where the multiple comes from.

**Where this corrects or extends the written summaries.**

- The caption contains no speaker introduction and never names the presenter. The content is the $100M Offers framework, the book is described as his, and he refers to 'one of our software companies that we sold called allen' (ALAN), all of which point to Hormozi presenting in 2022 ('what i'm doing…
- 'when the guys were spending 10 dollars a month they reached 300 000 people' is a caption corruption — the same passage later reads 'it says ten thousand right' and the arithmetic ('they'd make five thousand dollars off ten thousand') only works at $10,000. The $10 figure should not be used.
